Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-93, wherein the government is saying it is going to do away with organizations it really does not feel have any further use.
I would like to say that is not the case. Of the organizations listed in Bill C-931 want to concentrate on the changes to ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
It was not very long ago when Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation was set up by this government. Set up can be used in any way you choose. You can say that it was formed or put into existence as a transient measure.
When this government took office in 1984 regional development in Cape Breton was through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and through Cape Breton Development Corporation. The Cape Breton Development Corporation had two different parts. One was the coal division which looked after the coalmining industry and the other was the industrial development division. Funding was given to the industrial development division for industrial development on Cape Breton Island.
This government decided it wanted to shut down the industrial development division of Devco and would set up a corporation it would call ECBC, the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. This was supposedly to take over the operations of the industrial development division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Already in existence at that particular time was Enterprise Cape Breton which was put into place when DRIE, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, was done away with. We had Enterprise Cape Breton and now the government was setting up Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
It was not veiy difficult to see that the idea was to try to merge the two, get rid of one or both of them. The
government got rid of Enterprise Cape Breton. Now it is getting rid of Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. The regional development initiative, except for ACOA on Cape Breton Island, is going to disappear.
The fact of the matter is the government's statement that there is no need for this organization is absolutely false. Nothing could be farther from the truth. I do not know how the government can say this when the rate of unemployment on Cape Breton Island is worse now than when the corporation was set up initially. How can it possibly be said there is no further use for it when it is obvious, as people, the statistics and the people in government will tell you, that the need is greater?
What we are getting here is a sleight of hand against and at the expense of the people of Cape Breton Island.
This does not seem to be the attention that the people of Cape Breton or indeed any part of Canada should be receiving from their own federal government. To say that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is going to be able to pick up the activities of this organization is absolutely false. There is going to be a reduction of activity in industrial development on Cape Breton Island at a time when it is tremendously important to the region.
One example which is of significant importance is that under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act the agency is not allowed to own land. Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation is allowed to own land and it has two important facilities: one is Sydport Industrial Park in Point Edward just outside of Sydney; the other is the experimental farm on Cape Breton Island.
The industrial park is of tremendous importance. It is on tide water on Sydney Harbour offering rail siding and a particular access road. It also offers wharf space and a large area of land.
What in the name of Heaven is going to become of this park? Is it going to be turned over to the municipalities? We do not know for what use. We also have to recognize that the municipalities, being in the financial condition they are at the present time, are not in a very solid state to be able to take over this facility.
February 16, 1993

Even more important is the experimental farm. There is a provincial demonstration farm on the mainland in Kentville. This farm, operated by Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, deals with agriculture in its specific unique state in Cape Breton Island.
It has been proven that what is applicable in agriculture either through crops or animals is not necessarily applicable on Cape Breton Island. The climates are different, as well as the topography, the soils and the terrain.
The fact of the matter is there was no way of determining how to best attract agricultural activity to Cape Breton Island until this demonstration farm was put into effect. Now it has shown to be a tremendous success. It has increased the agricultural activity on Cape Breton Island tremendously and the government is saying it may have to close because ACOA cannot own land.
There has been discussion with the minister responsible for ACOA, who is also minister of fisheries. I think he is sympathetic to the continuation of this farm because of the success the farm has had. The fact of the matter is: Where is the initiative and the acceptance of Agriculture Canada to take over the operation of this farm? We have not seen it at all. The budget last year discussed the closure of ECBC and the fate of the farm, and the fact is we still do not have any initiative from Agriculture Canada.
It is not right that the people of Cape Breton Island should be treated in this cavalier fashion, particularly since the economic problems are so daunting. We have never had the fishery in a worse condition. Tourism is down because of the GST and gasoline prices and the very nature of tourism now in the United States. People are taking shorter vacations rather than the long family vacations they once were. The forestry industry has its difficulties. The steel industry is drastically reduced. The coal industry is reduced.
Now the government is saying it is going to take away the initiatives and the stimuli that Cape Breton should have in order to attract new industry. It is counterproductive to the best interests of the people of Cape Breton Island.
The government was told this when it did away with the industrial development division of Devco. It has been
Government Orders
told repeatedly of the consequences, yet it is steamrolling ahead with this conceived idea that the people do not matter.
The people do matter. If the government would recognize that the people matter and recognize what is good for Cape Breton Island, it would not do away with Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoy the opportunity of entering into this debate dealing with Bill C-93 and only regret that it had not gone to committee before Christmas. However, after a couple of days debate it is time now to move ahead and get it to committee so it can be dealt with in detail.
I rise to enlist the support of members of this House to ensure swift passage through second reading of the legislation which is before us. I am particularly interested in part (e) of the bill, the merger of the Procurement Review Board of Canada with the Canadian International Trade Tribunal.
This merger streamlines government administration through the creation of a new entity called the international trade and procurement tribunal, or ITPT, which will combine the strengths of the Cm and the PRB and report to Parliament through the Minister of Finance.
The merger also paves the way for an improved bid challenge mechanism that more suppliers of government procurement need that can be used to appeal contracts they feel have not been awarded fairly. In fact, the legislation positions the ITPT to meet all of the government's current and future bid challenge responsibilities.
For the short time that the free trade agreement has been in place and considering the limited scope imposed upon the PRB under the free trade agreement, the PRB has under the guidance of the former chairman, Gerry Berger, and the present chairman proved to be an inexpensive, speedy and even-handed alternative to the court system.
Indeed, they have set up an impressive set of laws, regulations and policies which ensure that suppliers will be dealt with fairly. Now suppliers seeking recourse when they feel they have been denied a fair opportunity to bid have found the PRB to be an extremely responsive vehicle.

Government Orders
In fact about 5,000 Supply and Service Canada procurements out of almost 300,000-about 2 per cent of our procurements each year-fall within the scope of the FTA. These are all potentially subject to the PRB and the PRB has handled some 95 complaints since its inception in January 1989. The majority of these were raised by Canadian suppliers who felt they had been unfairly treated.
Indeed, as a result of the decisions, if read, you will find that about one-third of those have been sustained to the point that they felt the procurement had not followed the rules laid down by government legislation and regulation. This gives a good opportunity for the suppliers to bring their complaints and indeed for procurement officers in various federal government departments to be more aware of how they should handle their procurements in a level playing field.
Suppliers tell us they are pleased with the transparency of this quasi-judicial review authority. It brings a good bit of honesty to the federal procurement system. They have also appreciated the board's informal and expedient approach. Complainants have felt that the PRB dealt with them fairly and they have appreciated not having to incur the time and expense of court hearings.
The board has given short shrift to frivolous complainants. It has not been used as a delaying or leveraging tactic, nor has it been used to distort the competitive market.
Similar to the Procurement Review Board, the guiding principles of the ITPT will be to promote an open, fair, impartial and transparent procurement process. The new tribunal will function in a timely and effective manner with the powers to receive complaints, conduct inquiries and to make determinations.
Naturally the ITPT would first assume the PRB's former role so that the merger does not disrupt the service to suppliers and Canada will continue to fulfil its obligation under the FTA.
However, many companies in industry associations have suggested that a similar form for redress should be available to suppliers on a broader range of federal procurements, indeed federal procurements which we make just within the government and are open to only
Canadian suppliers. The legislation before us opens the way to such a forum.
If we are truly committed to ensuring the integrity of fairness of government procurement then we must also be committed to ensuring that it is capable of withstanding independent third party scrutiny.
At the federal level we have already taken a number of steps, for example through the open bidding policy to achieve greater access, fairness and openness for all potential suppliers. Open bidding was an important and welcome development for suppliers. Simply put, more businesses can now access the federal market. There was nowhere to go to complain if one of them thought there was something wrong with the way the contract had been awarded.
The only avenues were through the departments, first of all to the procurement officer who perhaps awarded a competitor the contract, then to the deputy minister and then to the minister. With this new system the people will be able to direct it to an arm's length, third party tribunal, which will give them a fair hearing.
As I mentioned earlier, the first obligation under the FTA will be continued and then the broadened bid challenge mechanism would be introduced, which would encompass purchases covered by Supply and Services Canada's open bidding policy.
That is all the contracts which Supply and Services Canada puts out to tender of over $25,000. Generally speaking, that is good and makes sure that the playing field will be level for all suppliers. That amounts now to more than $4 billion annually that we opened up for challenge under this new mechanism.
We will set up this broadened bid challenge mechanism by establishing regulations that will allow appeals of these contract awards to the ITPT.
The introduction of such an appeal mechanism will be a landmark event for Canadian companies that supply goods and services to the federal government. It would challenge the whole federal procurement system to be squeaky clean.
Suppliers of commodities covered by the open bidding policy would then have recourse to the type of indepen-
February 16, 1993

dent bid challenge mechanism that suppliers of federal government requirements covered under the FTA now enjoy.
Later if Canada, the U.S. and Mexico ratify the North American free trade agreement or when the GATT introduces perhaps a wider scope and insists on an independent third party mechanism, the ITPT will be in a position to serve as a required bid challenge mechanism for contracts covered under the FTA, GATT, or any other international agreement.
In the case of NAFTA that chapter covers virtually all government contracts for goods and services with a value of more than $50,000.
Eventually most federal procurements, not just the portion carried out by my department but also that portion carried out by other federal departments, will be subject to ITPT scrutiny.
The new tribunal will retain the PRB's rapid response and informal hearings. I envision that for all but the biggest cases decisions will be made by one member rather than a panel. The preference will be for file hearings consisting of tribunal members' review of the government files. In other cases hearings could be conducted by telephone or through an exchange of letters. In fact in-person hearings would only be held when necessary, not as a matter of course.
The PRB approach of minimizing the need for lawyers will also be retained. Sorry about that. There will be no prerequisite to have legal representation before filing or proceeding with a complaint.
The experience with the PRB under the free trade agreement was the first for a Canadian bid challenge mechanism. It has taught us a lot. For one thing we saw that we did not have to follow the U.S. model which was complicated and adversarial, more closely resembling a court proceeding.
Instead we came up with a uniquely Canadian solution. We set up an informal tribunal with the power to investigate, to obtain relevant facts from the government and to conduct hearings in a non-adversarial climate that featured a refreshing absence of red tape. Suppliers and buyers have both gained from the PRB experience.
This does not mean that we cannot make mistakes. I have 1,600 procurement officers in Supply and Services.
Government Orders
We do over 1,000 contracts every working day. We in the department are very encouraged by this new process of open bidding and by the openness of the appeal mechanism which this legislation is going to put in place.
I encourage all members of the House to give speedy passage to this so that we can get it into committee and out of committee and in place so that the suppliers of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada, the industries in this country will have a way of making sure that there is a level playing field when they want to bid on federal government contracts.

Mr. Speaker, each day, each week, each year that passes the credibility of this government becomes more strained. Each budget the government brings before this House makes it more difficult for the people to believe that the government has any plan to get Canada out of the deficit-debt syndrome in which we find ourselves.
Each year for the last eight or nine years the government has told the people of Canada that it is raising taxes and cutting expenditures so that it can get rid of the deficit and start working on the debt. What has happened? Each year we have been promised that it would get the deficit under control but the level has stayed the same. We have had more taxes, we have had the GST, we have had a variety of taxes foisted on us. We have had cuts in every part of every department. It has had no impact on the deficit and the debt. In fact, the debt of Canada has increased to something over $400 billion from less than $200 billion eight years ago.
None of the policies, none of the cuts, none of the tax increases that the government has indicated as part of their policy, part of their planning, has made any difference to the level of debt. As economic predictors, as economic controllers, the government has been a total failure.
We come to Bill C-93. This bill is cited as budget implementation, as government organization. Among those changes are a number: Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, Agricultural Commodities Marketing Act, Agricultural Canada Opportunities Agency, the Canadian Council for the Arts has been changed to the Canadian Council for the Arts and for Research in Social Sciences and Humanities. It also changes things like the Intellectual Properties Act.

February 16, 1993
Government Orders
It is an omnibus bill which does a lot of little things but does nothing to improve the economy of Canada, nothing for the people of Canada and nothing to create more jobs. It does nothing to increase the agricultural funding that is necessary. Not one of the changes in this bill has anything to do with improving the economy of Canada; not one of these changes is aimed at increasing the effectiveness of the economy of Canada.
This is a case, as a former speaker said when speaking to this bill, of Nero fiddling while Rome bums. It is wide-ranging legislation which makes changes in the structure of a number of organizations that have given this government and previous governments good advice and made the people of Canada knowledgeable about why changes were being made, why the government was doing certain things, and putting before the government good reasonable kinds of changes which would improve the structure of economic development.
The wide-ranging changes that are being suggested now are not being suggested to increase the quality of economic decisions made by this government. It is not being recognized for economic reasons. The organizations that are being cut, pressed together, eliminated in this bill are being messed around with to the point where their basic thrusts in advising the government cannot be focused on the area where they have the most control. In fact, the intention seems to be exactly the opposite, to give the organizations which are being kept and added to such a broad focus that they will not be effective in any of their advice. While the debt keeps growing, while the deficit remains the same and while the economy continues to decrease, the number of jobless increases.
This bill will change the Canada Council for the arts to the Canada Council for the Arts and for Research, Social Sciences and Humanities. None of the communities involved by the agencies being affected have been consulted on this change. None of them were consulted when these changes were suggested initially by the Minister of Finance. If they had been consulted, the action would probably have been quite different.
Approximately 14 years ago, these two organizations, arts and humanities and social sciences, were separated
because it was recognized that one organization representing about 250,000 artists did not fit within the same area as an organization representing social sciences and humanitarian research in 100 or so universities and colleges across the country. The change to split the two organizations was carried out 14 years ago in consultation with the people involved, with the universities and with the artists of Canada. It was supported by both communities.
What has the government done now? It will tell you it is making this change to save money. However, its record is not good. The quality of previous organizations could have been kept and the cost reduced with the focus of those organizations kept upon the areas most concerned about advice being given to the government. The record of the government is not good because as it has made these cuts across the board with organizations of this type. The effective results of those cuts has not reduced the deficit but has reduced the effectiveness of the organizations. These two communities will not be well served by this division and possibly by the dilution of funding.
I suspect and so do both the arts and humanities and social sciences communities that the real aim of this amalgamation is to reduce the funding for both groups. Research funding has already taken major cuts. It is likely that this action and this bill will further cut research funding to the social sciences and humanities.
If the government's past record on effectiveness in reducing the deficit stays the same, we cannot expect anything but reduction in the effectiveness of the organizations and less value for the money that we do spend. Fourteen years ago there was no clear link between these two organizations. There is no clear link now.
It is time to get down to job creation, to effective agricultural policy funding. Now is not the time for doubtful and thoughtless changes with no real aim in improving the life of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to this debate and start with the general thrust of this bill.

February 16, 1993



I would like to borrow a parallel from the environment and reflect for a moment on how this government is beginning to act. Actually it has acted for some time like a dinosaur. This dinosaur is in a particular frame of mind, if it has any. The dinosaur is in the throes of death and is becoming dangerous to those it purports to govern, is in a demolition mood and in that mood is more and more voracious.
As you may recall, from when we debated Bill C-63, the dinosaur had already destroyed through that measure a number of very fine Canadian institutions. Among them was the Economic Council of Canada which was a very valuable tool to the government in providing policy alternatives in economic planning and development.
The dinosaur destroyed the Science Council of Canada. I do not need to describe its merits. I am sure everyone is well aware of what it did to inform Canadians about scientific thought and its development. It took some very valid initiatives.
At that time, and I am referring to November 30, 1992 when that bill was passed by the House of Commons, the Law Reform Commission was not spared by the dinosaur. Again I do not need to describe the merits of the Law Reform Commission, they were self-evident. It was providing the cutting edge of thought in penal reform.
The Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security was also a victim of that particular misbehaviour. I might add that the Centre for Ocean Development did not escape the rage of this particular government.
It was not enough for the dinosaur. The bill we are discussing today is the expression of its desire to demolish more. Today we are debating a measure which among other things would remove or abolish the Canada Council for Arts. Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that we have to go through closure and time limitation restraints on this because I think the time would be better spent in committee reviewing these changes in more detail. I would like to discuss aspects of Bill C-93 and will start with the Agricultural Products Board.
Bill C-93 provides for the winding up of the Agricultural Products Board. Over the years the board has provided the important service of stabilizing markets for agricultural commodities. We believe that function can be exercised more efficiently on the basis of an amended Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act with the support of the Department of Agriculture.
The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will now bring under its roof the ECBC which is Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The corporation will be dissolved and all of its rights, property and obligations will be assumed by ACOA. The ECBC programs will continue but there will be no duplication or overlap through the competing agency, ACOA. Those changes were tabled in the budget speech February 25, 1992.
Bill C-93 will also result in the creation of a new single cultural agency by combining the Canada Council and the Social Services and Humanities Research Council. I want to emphasize that despite fiscal pressures on our
government we have continued to provide significant levels of funding for the arts and humanities. We believe that Canadian culture has a vital role in fostering a vigorous and united nation, so those changes will be good.
The new council will deal with the full range of cultural matters including international cultural programs and international academic relations under the auspices of the Department of External Affairs. Under the provisions of the act the new council will be required to take Canada's foreign policy into account in fulfilling its mandate.
Also under Bill C-93 we propose to fold the Canadian Commercial Corporation, otherwise known as the CCC, into the Department of Supply and Services. The minister has just spoken on that so there is not much more to be said.
We are proposing an incremental dissolution of the CCC which would not be finalized until the Minister of Supply and Services is satisfied, as he mentioned this morning, that there will be no detrimental effects upon our exports or trade relations with other countries. In the interim the CCC will continue or remain a corporate entity.
Also under Bill C-93 we are taking a look at Emergency Preparedness Canada which began as a civil defence organization in 1948 with the Department of National Defence. Its title, mandate and structure changed a number of times during the first 40 years and EPC became a separate agency with the passage of the Emergency Preparedness Act in 1988 which replaced the War Measures Act.
As part of this initiative the government also proposes in part V of this bill that Emergency Preparedness Canada be folded back into the Department of National Defence. This is an appropriate action given the fact that EPC was housed with DND prior to 1988 and still reports to the Minister of National Defence.
Part VI of Bill C-93 provides for the amalgamation of the RCMP External Review Committee and the RCMP Public Complaints Commission into a single body entitled the Independent Review Commission for the RCMP. As was the case with the ERC and PCC, the new commission will be independent of the RCMP and will deal with public complaints concerning the conduct of
February 16, 1993

RCMP officers and review appeals and grievances from members of the RCMP.
Consolidating these two similar agencies will achieve savings in administrative overhead, eliminate duplication of services and allow for increased efficiency in program delivery, both to the public and to members of the force.
I encourage members of the House to support this bill and facilitate its speedy passage.
Part VII of Bill C-93 deals with the Intellectual Property Tribunal. Bill C-93 will encourage efficiency gains to be realized by merging the Copyright Board, the Trademarks Opposition Board and the Patent Appeal Board to form the new Intellectual Property Tribunal, otherwise known as IPT. Its duties will include the fixing of royalties which the performing rights societies may collect in return for granting licences for the performance of dramatic or musical works. The tribunal will also decide how royalties should be divided, including those generated by the retransmission of television and radio signals. The IPT will also arbitrate disputes and copyright royalties and decide opposition and cancellation proceedings arising under the Trademarks Act.
Part VIII of Bill C-93 deals with the International Trade and Procurement Tribunal. The bill provides for the merger of the Procurement Review Board and the Canadian International Trade Tribunal, otherwise known as CITT. Following the merger the new organization will be named the International Trade and Procurement Tribunal or ITPT and will report to Parliament through the Minister of Finance.
The Procurement Review Board was established under part II of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act in 1988.
Part IX of Bill C-93 deals with the Petroleum and Monitoring Agency. The government intends to wind up the Petroleum Monitoring Agency known as PMA. For those who are unfamiliar with the PMA, the agency publishes semi-annual and annual ownership surveys of the petroleum industry, as well as other reports as requested by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to whom it currently reports.
The Veterans' Land Administration is part X and the final chapter on this re-administration. It provides that
Government Orders
the Veterans' Land Administration Act be wound up and its functions and responsibilities transferred directly to the Department of Veterans Affairs. This merging of VLA operations with those of the department will allow greater economies while ensuring that the interests of veterans are fully protected.
In summary, these are administrative changes which will have a net saving for the taxpayers of Canada. That is something we all have to be conscious of because the cost of running government seems to be escalating when it should be shrinking. That is what we are now doing but not at the expense of the delivery of services; we are doing it to enhance the delivery of services.
I think most members in this House can take encouragement from that. If we look at the cost of government services in relation to our gross domestic product, it has grown dramatically in the last 15 to 20 years. It has to be curtailed, and I think part of that curtailment goes down to the efficiency and delivery of those services.

Now I would like to say something about the government's proposal to set up a new organization that would combine the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and the Canada Council.
As we know, this is an old idea. In 1978 the two councils did form one body, and after a great deal of discussion and consultation the decision was made to have two separate bodies, one to look after the arts and

Government Orders
the other to look after research in the social sciences and humanities.
It is surprising to see that the government is making this proposal. There are a great many objections to it. It is not only our caucus that objects but the educational and cultural communities also have numerous objections, especially as regards the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, which has done a great deal of work in the area of research. It is one of the best institutions of its kind not only in North America but anywhere in the world. It functions well, and academics connected with it have written to us to say that everything is going smoothly. Why is the government trying to break something that works? As they say in English, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".
The council says the government's proposal has not taken its views into account. There has been no consultation at all.
In addition, as we know, the government has decided to cut the budgets of these two organizations by 10 per cent. It is incredible to see the government on the one hand cutting funding to both councils and on the other trying to get rid of them by setting up a third.

Furthermore, the government's proposal does not take into consideration the question of representation for the two councils. What does the government propose? Is it going to appoint one representative for the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council side and one for the arts side? How would that work?
I find it truly bizarre that this proposal should be brought before the House of Commons without any consideration being given to the opinions of those who will be affected by the merger. We therefore suggest to the government that it at least set aside this part of the legislation, or that it agree to hold broad consultations with these bodies and especially with the most interested parties.
I do not think there is any need to push ahead so rapidly with this proposal. We have heard from a great many representatives of universities, student groups and professors, and I do not see how the government can go ahead with a proposal that everyone is against. The government should be asked: Who came up with this proposal? Who had the idea of merging, without consultations? What would the advantages be? Personally I do not think either of the organizations targeted by the proposal would derive the slightest benefit.

As a government, as politicians, we have a duty to take Canadians' views into account before we make decisions that concern them. For example, the government has to devote more effort to the research and development sectors and the councils working in the social sciences sector. We should also consult the Canadian Association of University Teachers and the various Canadian federations active in the humanities and in the social sciences. These are the groups that are particularly affected by the proposal, and the government has an obligation to consult them.
I have a letter from the Canadian Graduate Council, addressed to the Prime Minister. In it, the Council asks the Prime Minister to undertake just such consultations.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the debate today. However I am unhappy the debate is going on because I think it is entirely unnecessary. I think this is something long overdue.

Many people tell me that there are too many different branches of government, too much duplication of services and that is what this bill is really all about. It is eliminating a lot of the duplication, overlap and division of decision making that is seen. The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte did deal a little bit with emergency preparedness in Canada and the fact that today perhaps it has become a little bit redundant. Certainly most of the changes that have been recommended by the government are very worth while.
Emergency Preparedness Canada began as a civil defence organization in 1948 within the Department of National Defence. Its title, mandate and structure changed a number of times during the next 40 years. The EPC became a separate agency with the passage of the Emergency Preparedness Act in 1988 which replaced the War Measures Act.
Many people today are asking why do we need such a thing. The cold war is over. Yet as we consider the unstable nature of the world in which we live, the problems that develop periodically across the country, it is obvious that we still need such an organization.
As my colleagues have already indicated, we would like to take 15 of these separate bodies and consolidate them into 10 separate organizations. As part of this initiative, the government proposes in part V of this bill that Emergency Preparedness Canada be folded back into the Department of National Defence. This is veiy appropriate action, given that the EPC was housed within the DND prior to 1988 and still reports to the Minister of National Defence. I can see no reason at all for this to be a separate entity and this is an excellent move.
Some people are wondering what the function of the EPC is. It co-ordinates the development of civil emergency preparedness among federal government organizations, provincial governments and international organizations. In other words, it deals with all the various government bodies. It maintains a 24-hour a day nation-
Govemment Orders
wide watch of potential and actual emergencies. That is the key; not only will it deal with emergencies but it will attempt to anticipate anything that does develop.
This would be under the auspices of the Government Emergency Operations Co-Ordination Centre in Ottawa. The EPC would be headed by an executive director who is a public servant. Its head office is in Ottawa with regional directors in most of the provincial capitals and a permanent representative on the Canadian delegation to NATO in Brussels. Its annual budget is $20 million and approximately 100 people are employed by it.
The budget papers noted that EPC's function in relation to planning and co-ordinating civil defence preparedness remains essential. I agree 100 per cent.
However, its separate organizational status is not necessary for the effective fulfilment of its mandate. Moreover, folding the EPC back into the DND will allow for its function to be continued just as adequately at a much lower cost than administrative overhead. We all agree that having the decision making and the ability to carry out those decisions without consulting other organizations is essential and makes good sense.
Like a number of other measures in this bill, the action proposed for EPC is a modest one if considered in isolation. Yet by taking them together with the other proposals of Bill C-93, it represents the sustained efforts on the part of this government to streamline its operations wherever it makes sense to do so.
This is what my constituents have been telling me. Let us see you streamline government wherever you can. Let us cut out the redundant waste. This is an excellent part of this bill.
The other area of the bill that I would like to talk about briefly this morning is the Intellectual Property Tribunal. This is an international concern. Many nations are concerned about the use and control of intellectual property. This is where the big advances are being made and it is of concern to people when they develop ideas that they want some kind of protection. They want to receive the benefits not just from manufacturing automobiles, et cetera. When they come up with ideas I believe they should have support and receive the benefits obtained from their intellectual pursuits.

Bill C-93 would encourage efficiency gains to be realized by merging the Copyright Board, the Trademark Opposition Board and the Patent Appeal Board to form the Intellectual Property Tribunal or the IPT.
Its duties will include the fixing of royalties which the Performing Rights Society may collect in return for granting licences for the performance of dramatic or musical works. Mr. Speaker, I am joining in the debate today at this particular stage of the bill to voice my objection about a specific clause of Bill C-93. That objection is to the part II of the bill which would effectively dismantle the ECBC, the agency in Atlantic Canada in Cape Breton Island which has been primarily responsible for economic diversification on that particular island.
As a Cape Bretoner I certainly understand better than most in this Chamber the difficult time Cape Bretoners and indeed people in eastern Nova Scotia have had for most of the second half of the century in dealing with economic and industrial diversification.
Cape Breton Island held great promise in the past and I hope in the future will hold great promise again. The island was developed primarily for its mineral resources and its location. It is very close to the European markets. We had-and I underline had-rich fishing grounds. We had a vibrant steel industry at the turn of the century. We did not have one steel mill; we had more than one, we had two steel mills. We had one in Sydney and one over on the north side.
In the early part of the century we also had enormous exploitation of a valuable energy resource: the coal resource.
The island has been populated by a whole hodgepodge of individuals who have come from other places looking for a better life. Many of them have come from Scotland and moved over here in a number of different migrations. A lot of people of Acadian descent live on the island up in Cheticamp and down in Isle Madam. We have the Irish.
We have almost every mix of individual that late in the last century and early in this century came over to take advantage of the jobs that were being created in industrial Cape Breton down in the coal fields, in the steel mills and also on the seas fishing.
Cape Breton has been in decline perhaps longer than any other industrialized part of this country. Cape Breton held such promise. Going way back, the fortress of Louisbourg was established and is still down there and has been re-created. It was one of the first areas of Canada that was populated because it held great promise. For many centuries new Canadians have found their fortune in Canada by working the resources of that great island.
The people are a strong people. They come from strong stock. They do not seek to take from society; they just seek to work. That is all they want to do. They want to make a living, contribute, raise their families and they want their families to perhaps have better opportunities than they had.
My father was a coal miner. He is retired now. We grew up in the town of New Waterford where I guess everybody was equally as poor. We did not realize we were poor until we grew up and moved away and said that gee, by anybody else's standards we were poor. However, we were pretty rich because we had the right value system. We had a value system that had evolved

February 16, 1993

down on that island because of economic hardship, because of adversity.
It was a mentality that said individuals living down there had to rely on each other. If you did not rely on each other you were not going to survive. That is because in the early part of the century the Nova Scotia provincial governments and the federal government allowed the resources on Cape Breton Island to be exploited.
British firms came in and set themselves up. They bought the coal industry down there. They had the rights to the coal and kept the people in collar as they would say in Newfoundland. We had the company store, the only place you could get credit. They owned the houses, the public utilities and the water system. They owned everything. In short, to try to get enough money to raise your family you were literally owned by the coal company.
The strikes came in the early part of this century and blood was spilled on the streets down in New Waterford during one of the strikes. Bill Davis was shot during a strike and killed by the army which had been called in to quell the disturbance and put people back where they wanted to put them.
Cape Bretoners have grown to be a strong people. We do not want welfare. We do not seek to have anything other than the ability to eke out a living on that island.
In the sixties the coal industry was in great difficulty. The markets were gone. The British companies that owned the coal industry had squeezed every last penny out of it to ship somewhere else. It was not reinvested in that island and the industry was shutting down.
The Hon. Allan MacEachen, who used to be a member of this place and is now a senator in the other place, introduced a bill in this House. The bill was the Cape Breton Development Corporation Act. At that point in time there were two reasons for it.
One was to try to rehabilitate what was left of the coal industry on Cape Breton Island. Liberals of that time felt they had a fundamental responsibility through policy and through legislation to try to equalize the wealth of this country. It is a principle we still believe in.

It is a beautiful piece of property by anyone's standards and has probably some of the finest people that one would ever meet anywhere in the world. We are used to the adversity.

Political interference has been alleged in many of these spectacular collapses that we have in Atlantic Canada.
After years of this government dismantling systems that we had in place, what do we have? We have Cape Breton Island with 21 per cent unemployment. We have Sysco with about 450 employees. We have the Lingan colliery about to close down. We have problems with Lingan-Phalen. We have fish plants in Cape Breton that are closing. We have an island in despair.
This bill seeks to take it even further. The government was not content to do away with the industrial development division of Devco and put it under the ECBC. Now it is completing the circle in this bill. It is completing the loop that it set out on a few years ago and it is destroying this special agency to deliver special assistance for a special problem in the place that I come from and that is Cape Breton Island.
If the government was going to do away with this agency and it was putting proposals on the table to try to do things better so that the good people of Cape Breton Island, my fellow Cape Bretoners, could have some hope from these economic policies, then I would sit down, I would debate and I would listen. What the government has done is complete the loop. It has done something that I did not think was ever possible and that is, after eight years of government policy, try to break the spirit of the great people of Cape Breton Island. Therefore, I will not be supporting this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Dartmouth who was talking about the Cape Breton Development Corporation. I thought as he spoke, what an excellent example of how a government is out of touch. If you read
the bill before us, you will find that the explanatory note indicates the reason the Cape Breton Development Corporation is being folded into ACOA is that the purposes of the development corporation have been served.
If you go back to what those purposes were at the time of the inception of that corporation, you will find that they try to address the very substantial unemployment situation in Cape Breton. The unemployment rate at the time the corporation was established by the government was of the order of 16 per cent. Now I understand it is of the order of 23 to 25 per cent.
I use this by way of example because members will be aware that Cape Breton is not exactly in my bailiwick in terms of constituency, but it is in my area of interest in the sense that those people, like the people whom I directly represent here, are hurting because of the unfair measures of this government. I use this as just the latest example of that.
Here is a case where a region of the country with an unemployment rate of 23 to 25 per cent is being told, in print, by the government that there is no longer any need for the agency that was set up initially to address the unemployment situation.
It is worth looking at the title of this particular bill, Bill C-93, an act to implement certain government organization provisions of the budget tabled in the House of Commons on February 25, 1992. February 25, 1992 is almost a year to the day.
We are here a year later discussing the measures that were announced by the Minister of Finance at that time. That admission is itself a fairly revealing commentary on this government, on the mind set of this government. It is the latest proof, I say to the minister, that this administration holds Parliament itself in contempt, in much the same way that it holds the people of Canada in contempt.
We now know that the much repeated example of the 85 per cent of Canadians who said in every way possible, through letters, through petitions, through public protests, in every way available to them, they were unalterably opposed to the goods and services tax. Yet the government proceeded to implement that very unfair and very unpopular tax. It is another indication that this government holds people in contempt, holds the elector-
February 16, 1993

ate in contempt, has no respect for the concerns, for the opinions, for the views of Canadians across this country.
Here we are, a year later, about to get yet another budget from this administration, I suppose, though what that will do I do not know. It has already had eight or so of them and we are still in pretty much of a stew, indeed I think the stew is bigger and worse than ever before. We are about to get another budget from this administration, and still we find ourselves wading through the measures of the last.
Why is that? The answer is simple. You know the answer, Mr. Speaker. The answer is because this Parliament has not sat as it should have, because of the long periods when we have been out of this Chamber.
The government, because of its contempt for this Chamber, has not even seen fit to do the housekeeping and get its legislation through the House. We find ourselves a full year later trying to do what ought to have been done many months before.
Since it has been so long since this budget was brought down, almost a full year, it is worth reminding ourselves of some of the things that are in this budget. One of them is the tax measure whereby the government would reduce the personal income surtax. Nobody can knock a reduction in taxes.
With this government there is always a but. Even with this reduction the government managed to get it wrong. The government managed to show its hand. The government managed to treat unfairly the people who needed a reduction most.
Look at the table which is included in the budget documents entitled "Impact of Surtax Reduction". A family of four with two adults and two children and an income is $15,000 a year will get a reduction of $2 in the budget year.
For the full year 1993 the income tax deduction, because of this measure, is $8 for a family of four with an income of $15,000.
A family of four with an income of $100,000 will get an income tax reduction of $442. That one example is an indication of where this government's commitment, thinking and bias is. It is not with the ordinary people of this country.
Government Orders
The budget which we have now had for just about a year has failed most miserably on the issue of job creation. There is a crying need in this country right now for an administration, a government worthy of the name to address the number one issue. The number one issue identified in the polls as recently as last week is the need for employment generation.
While this government's policies are driving jobs out of the country and causing the permanent closure of plants right, left and centre we see nothing whatsoever that would replace those jobs. We do not see this government taking any serious initiatives or efforts to replace some of those jobs to get some of the 1.5 million jobless Canadians back to work.
I recall when this administration was in opposition its members made a great big fuss in 1982 because the unemployment numbers across the country had hit the 1 million mark. They launched a great campaign. The Minister of Forestry was part of that campaign. They launched a great campaign saying how scandalous it was that a full million people were without jobs across the country.
I say to him that 10 years later the figure is up to 1.5 million.

Mr. Speaker, as we have heard many times this morning, Bill C-93 is 84 pages long. You would think it was an economic program for the 1990s. In the 10 minutes I have I would like to suggest that it does exceedingly little in terms of making the Government of Canada more efficient and more protective of Canadian taxpayers' money.
For example, as you know there are dozens of departments. There are still something like 350 federal Crown corporations and agencies. The whole federal government shrieks to be streamlined; shrieks to be more efficient and more sensitive to Canadians. This bill will do very little to streamline the Government of Canada and save much needed money, scarce tax dollars for better purposes.
Part I of the bill talks about, and I quote from the note in the government's bill: "The purpose of this part is to wind up the Agricultural Products Board and transfer its function to the Minister of Agriculture and to the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act". That is part 1 of the bill.

February 16, 1993
Government Orders
Part II says and I quote: "The purpose of this part is to wind up the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and transfer its function to the staff of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency" and so on throughout the bill.
In other words, the government will take what appear to be stand alone agencies now and push them under the umbrella of some other existing agency.
I would like to deal with part III in the few minutes I have which purports to: " wind up the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and transfer its functions and its staff to the Canada Council, and transfer certain functions and staff to the Department of External Affairs concerned with the promotion of Canadian culture abroad to the Canada Council. Canada Council will be renamed the Canada Council for the Arts and for Research in the Social Sciences and Humanities to reflect its expanded functions".
There are six parts in the bill and they all do similar things. There has been a uniform outrage from people across the country about what the part I just referred to would do: the merger of the Canada Council and the academic funding boards.
I would like to quote from a letter although I will not name the person because I do not have permission. The person is at the University of Alberta and I am sure that she speaks for academics right across Canada. A part of her letter to the Prime Minister reads as follows: "I write with regard to the legislation affecting the merger of that council with programs from external affairs and with the Canada Council. The proposed merger of these three organizations has been effected without consultation with the communities of artists and scholars involved, nearly all of whom are opposed to it.
They are opposed for good practical reasons that are historically borne out. The scholarly and the artistic communities shared the first Canada Council when it was initially established and learned how inoperative that arrangement was. This legislation proposes to reverse the separation of the councils that was initially proposed to solve a problem.
It represents a step backward into the problems we had previously stepped out of; problems created by the veiy
basic differences between the work of cultural production in the performing of visual arts and scholarly research in the humanities and social sciences".
Finally she says: "Concerns of the research community about this merger are many. They include the failure of the present legislation to guarantee continued separate funding for the research and performing arts divisions of the new council. The failure of the legislators to consult the community of council users and the possibility-even likelihood given the description of the new council-the council's governing board will include significant members of patronage appointments with little knowledge of the arts or of scholarly research".
She asks for a reply from the Prime Minister. We will all wait with interest to see what the Prime Minister says particularly with respect to what his government has done to the academic community, to the teaching community and to equip young Canadians to compete in an emerging new world economy.
I do not have the time to go into it in detail, but I would just like to make three points that university teachers have made about post-secondary educational funding and federal research and development.
As my colleague said, this is what this group of dinosaurs opposite has done to the Canadian economy and young people in Canada since 1986. First of all, between 1986 and 1993 the established programs funding cutbacks will amount to $4.7 billion. That affects a lot of young people. That affects a lot of daughters and sons of a lot of members of Parliament and of course many other Canadians who are seeing post-secondary education suffer deeply at the hands of the members opposite. While they cut back $4.7 billion for post-secondary education and other programs including social programs, they have $4.4 billion available to purchase 50 submarine chasing helicopters.
What kind of priorities do these people opposite in this House have? Somebody pointed out that by not spending $4.4 billion on the submarines about 75 times as many jobs would be created if used in other more rational, more sane and more twentieth century methods.
February 16, 1993

Second, for the Tories to say that there is no money for post-secondary education when they almost instantly find the $4.4 billion I referred to for the submarine chasing helicopters is self-evident nonsense.
Third, why not institute tax credits to encourage our private sector to invest in basic research?
These people present themselves as bringing this bill before us to save taxpayers' money and make government more efficient but they have done no such thing since they took office. Canada's public debt is now about $665 billion and our foreign debt is about $300 billion. Not all of it has been hoisted on the backs of Canadians by this unloved government opposite. It is true that provincial governments have done it and the private sector has incurred debts.
A point was made recently by somebody in the private sector about the rapid deterioration in the deficit and debt to GDP ratios. In 1975 the total debt of the federal and provincial governments was 29 per cent of GDP. For those opposite, GDP means gross domestic product. In 1993 it has been estimated that the total debt in Canada will be at 96 per cent of GDP.
When will the IMF arrive in Canada? When will Japanese or Swiss investors stop buying our bonds? When will those opposite stop increasing the debt on the backs of Canadians by approximately $80 million to $100 million a day. Every 24 hours that go by, Mr. Speaker, you, your children and my children become further indebted by these people who constantly present themselves as being paragons of fiscal orthodoxy and fiscal concern.
It is like President Reagan who came into office saying he was going to fight the deficit and stop spending and borrowing money. I believe when he came into office the United States national debt was in the order of $700 billion. Today, at the end of the Reagan-Bush period of spend and borrow the U.S. federal debt is now in the order of about $4 trillion. Similarly these people opposite came into office saying they were going to fight the deficit and fight the debt. They have more than doubled the national debt of this government; $30 billion deficits through year after year after year. I will bet that if there is anybody on the other side who is prepared to get up to try to defend this bill, they will get up and say that they have been fighting the deficit and trying to protect the
Government Orders
Canadian taxpayer. It is all a lot of nonsense, as is this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I see that I only have about five minutes. I would just like to continue where my colleague left off on this particular bill.
As we know, this is primarily a machinery of a government piece of legislation. That means that the officials, under the name of efficiency, are trying to reorganize and make these government units more efficient. From that particular point, I support any effort by the government to try to make service to the public more efficient. I think it is incumbent upon all of us in this House to encourage the government to try to review various agencies, departments of government and Crown corporations to make sure that they are in fact meeting the public policy objective they were originally targeted to achieve.
The problem I have when we bring forward bills like this to the House of Commons is that they seem to take away from the real problem that is happening in our country out there. That is the deep pain that people are going through right now. We need legislation in this House that deals with putting people back to work.
I want to refer specifically to a bill we had in here last week, the Small Businesses Loans Act, where we on this side of the House co-operated with the government, put the bill through the House in one day and urged the government to bring it to committee so we can bring in some witnesses. We can then return that bill to the House and get it into third reading and pass it so that the
900,000	small businesses in this country that could or might be eligible to use the Small Businesses Loans Act can use it. That is where the real source and hope for new job creation lies in this country.
Overall, this is an omnibus bill in which we are putting all these various agencies of government together and transforming them and reorganizing them. Obviously, even if we did have some amendments here, the government probably would not accept them. It very rarely does. However, I am hoping that when we get through this particular piece of legislation we will get something back on the table that is more relevant in terms of the economy.

This is the kind of debate in this Eiouse today that really causes a lack of respect for the institution. Most Canadians do not even understand the purpose of these agencies and to exacerbate or prolong the debate is really not productive when it does not seem relevant to the real priorities which most Canadians feel we should be addressing at this point.
I wanted to mention, for example, part III of this particular bill where the government is winding up the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and transferring its functions and staff to the Canada Council. There was really no need for the government to make that machinery of government change.
This really was not going to improve the efficiency. One of the things that happens when you make all of these machinery of government changes or when you move these various divisions around is that quite often the effect it has on morale in a negative way outweighs the benefit that the government may attempt to achieve.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair until two o'clock pursuant to Standing Order 24(2).
The House took recess at 1 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec supports the federal government on the North American free trade agreement.
"The Government of Quebec is on the whole favorable to NAFTA,'' said the Liberal minister for international affairs, John Ciaccia, as he made public a 90-page study entitled Quebec and the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The authors of the study say that Mexico's inclusion in the free trade area will not fundamentally upset the
economic parameters that Quebec producers, exporters and investors must consider.
As far as agriculture is concerned, Quebec is pleased that NAFTA will not affect the Canadian supply management system for eggs, dairy products and poultry. The study also points out that Mexico offers attractive possibilities for producers of dairy cattle and bovine genetic material.
The new trade agreement respects Quebec legislation on the professions, consumer protection and financial services. Also, Quebec's language policy is not affected.

Mr. Speaker, last week the NDP premier of Ontario was handing out hundreds of billions of dollars for roads, sewers and subways. This is the same premier, the same NDP government that says it has no money for a program to train 100 people with disabilities for skilled employment as electronic technicians.
This cost-shared program of training, job placement and follow-up would repay its costs in just 30 months. Yet it keeps getting bounced from minister to minister in Toronto while people with disabilities willing and anxious to work are kept poor and dependent.
Perhaps NDP colleagues from Thunder Bay, Beaches-Woodbine, Spadina and Nickel Belt think it is just fine that the NDP government has money for pavement and pipes but not for people. Or maybe they can explain why Bob Rae and his government do not seem to believe that Canadians with disabilities deserve the same chance as anyone else to have their own job and earn their own income.

Mr. Speaker, beginning June 1,1993 the European Community will require that all exports of softwood lumber to the European Community be either pasteurised or kiln dried.
February 16, 1993

This action will dramatically affect exports of coniferous material including our manufacture of lumber and also all our manufactured products shipped in packing crates, packing cases, drums and any kind of lumber.
The industry believes that the reasons for this restriction are not legitimate and amount to technical trade barriers which will impact a great deal of our exports to Europe including lumber and other products.
This initiative is a foreign government initiative and not supported by the industry in related European countries.
The industry is calling on the Minister for International Trade, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Forestry to give this issue the highest priority. It is asking for an extension of the deadline to allow its arguments to be heard in the short term and a total removal of these restrictions in the long term.

Mr. Speaker, many Manitobans are concerned and disappointed that new exploration for gold is being allowed in Shoal Lake, Ontario, Winnipeg's drinking water supply.
The commitment to do an environmental assessment of any future mine development should the exploration prove positive is not good enough. Personally, I take the view that the time has long passed when mining in the water supply of 600,000 people should be considered at all.
The conflict between Manitoba and Ontario on this issue points out the crying need for a national safe drinking water act, something the federal government has promised for years but never delivered, despite numerous attempts by individual members such as myself, the member for Skeena and the member from Beaches to encourage such action through private members' bills.
I call on the government to bring forward draft legislation in this area and in the meantime to look at whatever other ways might exist for it to intervene in this interprovincial dispute that is pitting short-term economic goals in one province against the long-term health of another.

Mr. Speaker, tobacco smuggling has taken on huge proportions in Canada. Over the years, the provincial and federal governments have dramatically increased taxes, which makes Quebecers and Canadians obtain their supplies on the black market and thus break the law.
I ask the Government of Canada to take the initiative of meeting representatives of the Quebec government to reassess the whole tobacco taxation system and recover the governments' revenue shortfall, because the public rightly feels exploited.
The governments know that some native bands are responsible for smuggling tobacco, liquor and drugs. Astronomical amounts of money are involved. It seems that organized crime which provides some outlaw groups with millions of dollars is tolerated. When will these people pay their taxes like any other citizen of Canada and Quebec?
Smuggling is in federal jurisdiction. The authorities and RCMP should thoroughly investigate these illegal activities. Ending all this illegal traffic on certain reserves may remove their opportunity for investing in the Charlevoix casino. Is that the way to launder dirty money?

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of the 11th report of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.
The committee recommended that the definition of serious harm be extended from severe physical injury or severe psychological damage to include any permanent or long-term disability, disfigurement or significant reduction in the quality of life.
These changes would reflect the serious harm done to victims of violent crimes under the age of 18 who must be

February 16, 1993
protected from dangerous offenders. I urge the Solicitor General to accept these recommendations and to bring forth appropriate amendments.
I also urge the Solicitor General to bring forth amendments to make the current system of dangerous offender applications less complicated and less likely to be plea bargained away.
Such amendments would include allowing a judge to bring forth an application and allowing Crown counsel to introduce such applications for persons convicted of violent crimes who are known to be high risk or repeat offenders.
To the Solicitor General I say, enough talk. Canadians and their families demand action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, few in this House have doubted the need for reform of the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Growth of our small businesses is being hindered by limited access to loan capital. Last week the suspicion was reinforced by the comments of the director general of the small business office of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. Mr. Ian Donald was reported in The Globe and Mail as saying that the banks are still hesitant to lend to small firms.
This statement reaffirms that today's entrepreneurs are indeed being squeezed by a reluctance to provide start-up cash and operating and expansion capital. It also points to the necessity of extensive changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act.
What concerns me is that the amendments to the SBLA in Bill C-99 do not yet address the problem of capital access while still leaving the program affordable to its applicants. Further changes must be made to this bill at committee or report stage.
We cannot lose sight of the fact that the growth of a number of our small businesses and the creation of new jobs for a number of Canadians in this sector are counting on these changes.

Mr. Speaker, on February 5 The Thunder Bay Times-News published an article predicting the eventual closure of CN's north line in northern Ontario.
It is totally irresponsible for the Thunder Bay-Atiko-kan NDP MP to fuel such speculation and to spread such gloom and doom. Has he thought for just one moment of the tremendous negative impact such a statement has had on the lives of the workers, the citizens and the communities along that line?
Hornepayne is a railroad town totally dependent on CN for its survival. Haavaldsrud's Lumber used the CN line to transport 12,000 tons of wood chips to Thorold last year as well as one-third of its lumber production. Weldwood of Longlac ships 80 per cent of its products on this north line.
Those affected demand that CN categorically deny the closure of this line and dissipate any uncertainty surrounding the issue. Further isolating these communities spells despair and disaster.

Mr. Speaker, the European Community is at it again, this time using technical barriers to keep our softwood lumber in any form out of its markets.
If left unchecked, this provision would become effective June 1, 1993 and would result in the loss of $1.4 billion in trade. I urge the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Forestry to continue strong representation on behalf of the softwood lumber exporters to derail this very restrictive practice. It cannot be allowed to succeed at the expense of our own Canadian industry.

Mr. Speaker, several labour groups, as well as the farmers represented by the UPA, have been working for a long time to set up an ethanol plant in Varennes, in the labour minister's riding.
February 16, 1993

This project is very important for the region's economic development. It could create more than 300 jobs directly and indirectly and increase the market for com growers in the region south and east of Montreal by 10 to 15 per cent.
In addition, ethanol is a product with a good future. It reduces environmental pressures and ethanol production is growing very rapidly in Ontario and Western Canada with the federal government's help.
I ask the Minister of Labour and member for Vercheres to act quickly so that this project can be carried out as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Scholarships Program has been a tremendous success. Thousands have received scholarships which are divided equally between men and women. One must have exceptional marks to qualify and maintain high grades to continue to receive the scholarships every year.
We have an opportunity through this program to measure educational results across the country by requiring applicants to take a standardized test.
I urge the minister of science of technology to consider holding tests for applicants. This will give us as Canadians an indication of how well our educational systems are performing across the country.

Mr. Speaker, 1,600 Canadians asked me to present a petition to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The petition asked her first to urge the Government of Guatemala to negotiate in good faith with the real representatives of the Guatemalan people, including the Maya, to end the civil war.
Second, it asked that Canada tell all Latin American governments that we insist on having Guatemala registered under item 12, grave and systematic human rights violations, at the next meeting of the United Nations Human Rights Commission.
On January 20 I saw 2,500 Guatemalan refugees returning from Mexico in peace, the first of 45,000 yet to come. This happened partly through the pressure of the Guatemalan people and partly through negotiations by the Governments of Canada, France, Sweden and Mexico.
I commend Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada's part in this good beginning. I urge her to continue support for the refugee return peace negotiations with the URNG and United Nations monitoring under item 12.

Mr. Speaker, there is something radically wrong when we have people suffering from hunger in this country and we do not have a delivery system to get free food to them when it becomes available.
It is even worse when we have people actually dying of starvation in other countries and we cannot come up with a delivery system to take free food from Canada and put it into the hands and stomachs of these people.
The case in point involves 2 million hundredweight of P.E.I. and New Brunswick potatoes being diverted from the tablestock market through a federal-provincial agreement. These potatoes must be removed from the regular market.
Farmers in P.E.I. and New Brunswick do not want these potatoes to go to waste. They would very much like to see them used to alleviate hunger in Canada and abroad. Twenty million 10-pound bags of potatoes is a lot of potatoes and would feed a large number of people.
I would ask the federal government to use the resources at its disposal to make sure that as many of these potatoes as possible find their way into the plates of the hungry and starving in Canada and abroad rather than simply being allowed to rot and to be ploughed down in the fields.

February 16, 1993
Oral Questions POLITICS

Mr. Speaker, clearly concerns about racism, sexism and anti-Semitism can be relative in politics.
Everyone knows that the member for St. John's West has a histoiy of thoughtless, even tasteless loquaciousness masquerading as humour. He is an easy target even for arrows from within glass houses.
Within such a house resides Jean Pelletier who, uncondemned, counsels racial exclusion. Also there now is his friend Camil Samson who accused Jewish abortionists of trying to destroy the people of Quebec while elevating Hitler's economic policies.
Meanwhile in the Victoria men's room of the same glass house the defender of a rapist is in while two female executive members are out in the sexist cold.
The Liberal house is the house of glass; it is silent within, with an interesting cast.

Mr. Speaker, this month the government missed an important deadline. By February the government had promised to complete studies of the first 33 chemicals on the priority list of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Only 5 of the 33 chemicals have been assessed. In other words, the majority of chemicals have not been assessed for their toxicity as planned.
Every day 1.5 tonnes of persistent toxic chemicals enter Lake Ontario. Therefore, the fact that many of these chemicals are still to be assessed and regulated is of extreme urgency. The government will not meet its own goal in the green plan where it promises to virtually eliminate discharges of persistent toxics in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River. Environment and human health are endangered because this government fails to keep its promises.

Police forces across Canada are to be commended for publishing the names and photographs of dangerous offenders who are
scheduled to re-enter the community. Canadians are entitled to learn the identities of those individuals who are considered to pose an extraordinary risk to public safety.
