speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question. Yesterday, the Minister for International Trade met with his Mexican counterparts and after the meeting, he did not say clearly what the government's position is and suggested that the government might proceed with the North American Free Trade Agreement without waiting for the results of negotiations with the Americans on labour, the environment and even agricultural problems.
Would the Prime Minister not agree to tell his minister that we should not proceed with the agreement in this House unless and until we know the results of the negotiations with the United States on the parallel accords that President Clinton wants?

Mr. Speaker, President Clinton already said, as I repeated yesterday, that the free trade agreement was a standalone document and that supplementary agreements would not in any way change the substance of the primary agreement. Supplementary agreements will be negotiated with Canada and Mexico in due course without affecting the accord itself. This means that we can proceed without compromising anyone's principles.
As for my friend's question, I would point out the position stated yesterday by Quebec's minister for international affairs, the Hon. John Ciaccia. He warned those like the federal Liberal leader who want to renegotiate
February 16, 1993

portions of the agreement or include new chapters in it. Mr. Ciaccia thinks that this might endanger this agreement which Quebec needs. Not only Quebec but Canada needs it. I think that Mr. Ciaccia, a former deputy minister of the opposition leader, was right and it would be time for him to listen to him again.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the minister of external affairs for Mexico said that this accord is perfect, that they will never look at reopening any element of it and more or less said that they did not take seriously the problems that President Clinton and Vice-President Gore mentioned on the environment.
Does the Prime Minister not realize at this time that this take it or leave it attitude will lead to a big problem and that it would be wise for this government not to rush into the House of Commons with a proposition? We should know exactly what the position of the American administration will be before taking the time of Canadians on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, we do know the position of the American administration. The position of the American administration was given in a statement by the President of the United States on Friday, February 5. In response to a question I indicated, and I quote: "The President has indicated many times that he is going to sign the NAFTA agreement as it is. But he proposes to bring in supplemental agreements with Mexico, particularly in regard to some of the points that he has mentioned that do not impact on the NAFTA agreement as concluded. President Clinton said: "That's right".

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, President Clinton said very clearly at the end of his intervention that he believes he can do that. He also said that he has to have included some parallel accord. It was exactly what was said last week by Mr. Kantor, who said that the administration will not present the deal to the American congress until it has these parallel accords.
Would it not be wise for this government to know what will happen in the United States before forcing a vote in this House, subject perhaps to coming back later to
Oral Questions
amend the legislation because there will be some supplementary agreements and the House will have to vote yes or no on them as well.
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition says that President Clinton went on to say something-
No, you don't.

Of course he said no such thing. I will read the transcript for my hon. friend. After, President Clinton said: "That is right". He then said: "And I might add that the Prime Minister's administration in Canada has had a strong record on the environment".
Oh, oh.
It makes sense to me.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition asks a question suggesting that the answer is there and indeed it is. I did not mean to offend the opposition, but it gets better.
Then President Clinton said: "Something that we want to try to beef up in the supplemental agreement, and that Canada would be, more or less in line with the United States in terms of its impact on any supplemental labour accord we might reach. We certainly intend to work with them. After all, this is a three way agreement, not a two way agreement". Then the President said: "But I still believe, as I said many weeks ago, that we can negotiate agreements without reopening the NAFTA itself".

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
About one hour ago, the minister announced that Canadian troops would be redeployed into Sarajevo. She added that there would be no new mandate, no air cover, no new equipment and no contingency plans. Yet she maintained that: "All possible measures had been taken to ensure the safety of the Canadian peacekeepers".
Considering that in the last few months 28 UN peacekeepers have been killed in Bosnia-Hercegovina, can the minister explain what kind of measures will be

February 16, 1993

taken to ensure that our troops are not being put at undue risk?

speechtext:

We are pleased to say that the 2nd battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment is perhaps one of the best equipped and able forces in that area of Yugoslavia at the time.
There will be a technical briefing on this deployment at 3.30 p.m. in conference room D at the Department of National Defence. speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what my colleague the hon. Secretary of State for External
Affairs was referring to was that she would like to see the international community take those steps.
She and I had the opportunity to attend a very useful and interesting conference on these matters in Munich a week and a half ago where all of our colleagues in Europe in particular and our American counterparts were addressing themselves to the question of what the future would be of the international community in addressing aggression and in trying to make sure the situation such as that in Yugoslavia did not spread and did not destabilize the rest of the world.
This is all being done through the United Nations. There is absolute consensus on the part of the government, and I think probably all members of this House, that the challenge we face now as members of the international community is to define the rules and principles by which we will join with other countries in trying to stop aggression and trying to prevent the development of a world where no country feels safe on its own, where all countries feel they have to arm themselves to the teeth because the international community cannot act to protect them.
This is the challenge we face today and this government is committed to addressing that challenge.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
This government is well aware of the concerns of Canadians with regard to environmental sustainability yet the NAFTA contains no guarantees to ensure that market forces cannot erode environmental standards, standards that are designed to protect the health and safety of workers as well as protecting the environment.
It contains no guarantees with regard to a country which fails to establish and enforce such reasonable environmental standards, which has in essence a trade subsidy.
I ask this government how it can continue to give assurance to Canadians that the interest of multinational companies will not override the democratic rights of Canadians.

February 16, 1993

Mr. Speaker, much of the information conveyed to the House by my hon. friend is of course inaccurate in regard to the proposed treaty as it affects the environment. In fact NAFTA was the first international trade treaty to deal with the environment and there is much to commend it to my hon. friend.
The members of the NDP are complaining. The NDP minister for development from Saskatchewan, Mr. Dwain Lingenfelter, said: "Western Canada and agriculture probably have more to gain from NAFTA than any other part of Canada".
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, that was an interesting non-answer. The minister he is referring to came back, in fact, more determined to oppose NAFTA than he was before.
That is right. And he said so publicly.

Will the Prime Minister give us his assurance of a parallel environmental accord? No parallel environmental accord can adequately address the concerns. Minimum acceptable environmental standards must be negotiated within NAFTA, not alongside it. We British Columbians have learned this to our sorrow.
Under the current trade deal, a conservation program that protected dwindling B.C. salmon stock was struck down as unfair to American trade.
My question is: If the government agrees to negotiate with the U.S. and Mexico a parallel accord, will it be negotiated in secret like NAFTA? Will it be a secret dispute settlement mechanism like NAFTA or will it be toothless, like it is now?

This government is condemning Canada to an environmental deficit. What we have had so far is an in-house, secret environmental assessment.

I want to make another point that is extremely important in regard to this debate. The member is making the argument that a developing country should have tariffs imposed upon it if it does not meet certain environmental standards.

trade with Bangladesh, Somalia and all the other developing countries in the world. I do not think that is in the interests of Canada, which is a trading nation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
The minister is aware that 25,000 people in eastern Bosnia are cut off in the town of Cerska while a UN convoy of food and medical supplies is parked on the side of the road just 20 miles away.
In Somalia we learned it was necessary to use force against the warlords to deliver supplies to the people most in need.
On Sunday the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested that Canadian peacekeepers should take a more active role in the region.
Does the redeployment of the second battalion which she announced today mean that the government is considering military intervention as a possible solution to the standstill of humanitarian relief efforts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer to that question is no. The 2nd battalion of the Royal Canadian Regiment is being deployed on the basis of what we call a permissible environment, which means it will perform its task of attempting to deliver humanitarian aid only with the acquiescence and co-operation of the other forces that are there. We see no reason at this time to change that mandate.
I think the hon. member would agree that the circumstances in Bosnia-Hercegovina are very different from those in Somalia. We are hopeful, as a result of the clarification of the American position with respect to Bosnia-Elercegovina, that co-operation will be found. We will be able to fulfil our task of delivering much-needed aid to starving people in that region of the world.

My supplemental is for the same minister.
On Sunday the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced that she wanted our Canadian troops to take a more active role in peacekeeping and peacemaking and that the rules of the engagement be absolutely clear.
Today the Minister of National Defence makes a confusing commitment for an additional 1,200 troops without consulting Canadians through a debate in this House. Troops cannot do their job properly if they are not given a clear mandate and a clear mission. There is a confusing mandate coming from the secretary of state, the Prime Minister and the present minister.
Will the Minister of National Defence stand up in this House today and give the troops going there a clear mandate and a clear mission as to exactly what they are to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only confusion appears to be in the mind of the hon. member.
The troops that have been redeployed today have been in that region since last November.
The original request from the United Nations to have them deployed in the Banja Luka area was not able to be fulfilled because our people were not able to get into that region. The United Nations has now asked us to redeploy in an area west of Sarajevo. We have accepted that engagement and our people are now on their way to fulfil that engagement.
Their mandate is very clear. There is not time in the context of Question Period to go into the details of it, but I would invite that hon. member to attend a technical briefing at the Department of National Defence at 3.30 p.m. today in which he could be advised of all of the specific aspects of that mission.
It is very explicit and I assure the House there is no confusion in the minds of the Canadian men and women who will be carrying it out.

Mr. Speaker, a newspaper headline on November 3 reads: "Canada wrong to send troops to former Yugoslavia says general". In this article two generals serving in the Canadian forces questioned the manner in which we commit our troops to peacekeeping operations. Later,
February 16, 1993

serious questions on command and control of peacekeepers were raised.
Can the minister still deny, as she did in Question Period yesterday, that serving generals are so concerned about this government's handling of peacekeeping commitments that they have seen fit to speak out in public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am only aware of one general who has made a comment of that sort and that was the general from whom we took advice on the acceptability of the risk to our people who were serving in Sarajevo at the time.
I think it is important to point out that the assessment of risk, the assessment of the appropriateness of the deployment of our forces and their ability to carry out the missions is an assessment that is undertaken not by politicians, but by expert military advisers.
The government then decides on the basis of that expert military assessment whether it is consistent with our foreign policy objectives to deploy troops in that particular way.
We have always been extremely respectful of the advice of our military advisers. I am not aware of anyone wearing a uniform of the Department of National Defence who is not supportive of the decisions that we have made because they know that they are based on the very best military advice.

Mr. Speaker, I think the minister has completely missed the point.
Clearly there is a problem with the way we commit Canadian troops operationally. Last fall the Chief of Defence Staff said that Canadian forces were stretched to the limit and that we could not sustain the current peacekeeping mission without additional resources. Two months later the new CDS said that reducing manpower was a defence priority. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot do more with less.
Will the minister recognize the reality of the serious situation and debate on the floor of the House of Commons Canada's involvement in peacekeeping and the manner in which we commit our troops?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome not only a discussion of that very important issue in this House of Commons, but in Canada as a whole.
As I have indicated since I became Minister of National Defence, peacekeeping requires the participation of a highly-trained, well-equipped professional military. It is not simply a question of boy scouts with guns. It is an extremely serious enterprise.
We deploy in this particular enterprise the resources that are available to us. Canada now participates in peacekeeping operations in 15 locations around the world.
It is quite true that we cannot continue to accept engagements and I think that with the growing capability of the United Nations we will be asked to accept more engagements. Therefore, I would ask all members of this House to think very seriously about what is an appropriate level of the Canadian military, what is an appropriate level of the defence budget, how many of these kinds of engagements we can undertake, consistent with what Canadians are prepared to pay to support their defence establishment.
Those are the questions we have to address. They are questions for all Canadians to consider because I think all Canadians support the need to contribute to creating a stable world order. How big a role Canada should be playing is one which we all have to address.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday in responding to questions, the Prime Minister reminded the House of the government's record in appointing women to key government positions to advise this government on important matters of the day.
One of those women, a woman who all members of the House would acknowledge as an outstanding Canadian, has said of the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act: "I am very concerned. I am concerned about the consequences of the law and by the minister's stubbornness in not seeing those consequences".
Would the Prime Minister agree to listen to and act on the concerns of his own appointee, Senator Solange Chaput-Rolland and put an end to this act?

Mr. Speaker, I have the greatest of respect for the opinions of Senator Solange Chaput-Rolland.
She is a very distinguished member of the Senate. She has well developed opinions on matters of public policy, some of which I endorse and few of which I do not. That will not surprise my hon. friend.
The reforms being proposed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration deal fundamentally with a very simple matter. In this society with the fiscal problems this country has, is it appropriate that someone who quits his or her job without reason, without excuse and without provocation, continues to draw unemployment insurance benefits paid for by his or her fellow Canadians? That is the issue.
That action is not insurance against unemployment. That action might fall under some other social program that my hon. friend would want to propose but it does not follow that every person who quits his or her job is entitled to payment by his or her fellow Canadians. That is the issue before the House and I think we have made the proper and intelligent decision under the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, Senator Chaput-Rolland, members of the government backbenches, certainly the opposition parties and many concerned Canadians understand something the Prime Minister does not, obviously.
Any Canadian who quits his or her job without just cause is already subject to a severe penalty today in this country. The real question the Prime Minister ought to address is: Is it appropriate in a country that has 1.6 million Canadians unemployed, and all the consequent misery for men, women and children in Canadian households, to battle unemployment by declaring war on unemployed Canadians?
February 16, 1993

Is that appropriate, or is it more appropriate to take measures to put Canadians back to work? Will the Prime Minister come to his better senses?

Mr. Speaker, this is an astonishingly misleading statement by my hon. friend, a very misleading statement.
The fact of the matter is that Canada treats its unemployed citizens more generously than any other G-7 country. Now my hon. friend might wave.
Talk about the penalty.
Thlk about the penalty. The penalty is the same, for example, as exists in New Zealand and as exists in France.

This is a self-inflicted difficulty of someone who without reason, without justification, decides he is going to quit his job.
It does not cost him a cent.

My hon. friend should be aware that in Canada, for example, we spend four times as much per capita on our unemployment insurance scheme as in the United States of America. It is so generous that there are some experts, including the House royal commission in Newfoundland, that suggested the present unemployment insurance scheme, as argued in Newfoundland, has distorted the ethic of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador and has added 2 percentage points-
Oh, oh.

That is an argument that has been made. It has added two full percentage points to the unemployment rate in Canada.
This country treats the unemployed with a level of generosity unmatched anywhere in the OECD, but we do not have an obligation in this country to provide someone who quits his job without reason, without provocation and without excuse with unemployment insurance paid for by fellow citizens. I think the decision of the Government of Canada has been an appropriate one.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will know that government's underlying policy as far as tobacco use is concerned is to try in every way, shape or form to reduce and eventually eliminate the use of tobacco products in this country.
We have taken cigarette smuggling, as a very serious issue. We have put in place numerous projects already, including joint efforts with the RCMP. Period the Prime Minister in responding to my question made reference to the House report and I believe made reference to a distorted work ethic in Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate again in the debate regarding Bill C-93 and in particular some of the effects that this bill will have on different agencies and different structures of the Government of Canada.
On an earlier occasion I took the time to spell out for the House the ways in which I believe this bill has been inappropriately laid before the House. At that time I indicated clearly that I thought this bill, which affects numerous departments and agencies of the Government of Canada, ought to have been split. However, the Chan-in its normal wisdom did not see the validity of my arguments and of course ruled otherwise.
Notwithstanding the aforesaid I do wish to reiterate for members of this House that there is one section of the bill in particular which is of great concern to my constituents. It has to do with the gutting of what has become known as Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
I know my colleagues from Nova Scotia, particularly the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, will want to support me in my endeavours in this particular debate. That hon. member was a part of a government on an earlier occasion which brought in legislation to create Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. I am certain that the hon. member in question would not want to be classified or referred to in the political world of Nova Scotia as a person who does not support the principles
for which he voted only a year or two ago and now would change because of the political winds a certain minister or a couple of ministers would have on the situation.
Now that I have the support of my colleague from Annapolis Valley-Hants I am wondering if perhaps we could get the support of the hon. member for South Shore who has been very studious in his representations on behalf of his constituents. I am sure that even though his political persuasion is different from mine he can readily see the merits of the proposals which I will lay before the House in a moment or two.
Years ago under the auspices of the Cape Breton Development Corporation two divisions were designated. One was a coal division, which is self-explanatory. The other was an industrial development division, the sole purpose of which was to try to expand upon the economic base in industrial and rural Cape Breton.
In 1988 the government of the day, to which members opposite are privy to, passed a piece of legislation, namely Bill C-103. In effect it did away with the industrial development division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
In its place members opposite, and in particular the Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, that other famous person in the upper house, Senator Murray said in no uncertain terms that this particular enterprise would assume the role of the industrial development division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
Now just a little anecdote about the great, famous Senator Lowell Murray. He comes from New Waterford, an area in my district of Cape Breton-East Richmond, but he is a senator from Ontario.
However back in 1988 when the good senator, supported by those left-wing pinkos of the New Democratic Party, passed Bill C-103 he said the following, which is from page 3656 of the Senate debates of June 14, 1988:
Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation will be a Crown corporation. It has a mandate almost identical to that of the industrial development division of Devco. As a Crown corporation, it will have a board of directors which-and I make this as a general statement-will have the same mandate and powers in respect to the ECBC as the board of directors of Devco has in respect of the IDD.
February 16, 1993

That was the great senator in 1988 when he travelled in Nova Scotia and in particular the three federal constituencies in Cape Breton and talked about this new wonderful identity called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
However, now we have on the floor of the House of Commons the Government of Canada under the auspices of the Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency placing before the House a bill which will do away with Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. It is the same argument the Liberal Party made during the entire debate on Bill C-103, which it opposed at that time for the very fear that this would be done away with within a short period of time.
I am sad to say to my colleagues opposite that they did have the support of the New Democratic Party with regard to Bill C-103. Perhaps not knowing the area or not understanding the complexities of the economic situation there, that is their rationale for supporting it, but I hope the New Democratic Party will come alive with its so-called common sense and support the provisions we are trying to put forward in that we ought not to destroy Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. We ought to keep it in place.
What is even more devastating in recent weeks is that the Government of Canada, not the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, not hon. members in our caucus, but the Government of Canada through the auspices of Statistics Canada has said to the people of Canada that the unemployment rate in industrial Cape Breton is 27.6 per cent. Is there any more justification for a federally owned Crown corporation to disperse economic development in that region? What other facts would hon. members need to affirm my conviction?
The action of this government in doing away with this Crown corporation will be met in the next federal election. It will be met in the next provincial election, whenever it is called. The premier of the province, just to show how bent, unfocused and removed the premier of Nova Scotia is with regard to economic development in Cape Breton, has said very little if anything with regard to restoring this agency and thereby putting pressure on the Government of Canada.
We know the track record of one Donald Cameron, premier of Nova Scotia. He set a precedent which is being followed by the private sector throughout Cape
Government Orders
Breton. The example I share with the House is that not less than two weeks ago Premium Automotive Tanks in Port Hawkesbury tried to lock its doors in the middle of the night and to escape into the darkness. It was following the actions of Premier Don Cameron, who did the same thing when he removed the toll booth from the Canso causeway a year prior to that.
I urge members of this House to stand in opposition to this particular bill. I give notice to the Chair and I give notice to the Thble that we intend as an opposition party to seek witnesses at the committee stage of this bill to examine in its entirety the consequences not only on Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, but also on all of the agencies which have been named therein. I seek the guidance, the support and the fairness of the Chair in making certain that particular operation is given a full hearing at the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, in the limited time at my disposal I will try to clarify the proposals before us in this bill, which might perhaps be called an omnibus bill since it deals with a number of familiar agencies: the Agricultural Products Board, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the Canada Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, Emergency Preparedness Canada, the Independent Review Commission for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Intellectual Property Tribunal, et cetera.
I would like to focus on the proposal to abolish the independence of one of the most dynamic bodies we have in the area of research, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. It is not a Johnny-come-lately. It was founded in 1978 by a Liberal government. The research it has funded in the social sciences has contributed greatly to understanding the importance of research in Canada, truly Canadian research, in very complex and difficult areas.
The bill before us provides for the dissolution of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the transfer of its functions, and of course its staff, to the Canada Council. The responsibilities of the Department of External Affairs for culture and education in the sphere of international relations would also be transferred to this new agency, which would be called the

February 16, 1993
Government Orders
Canada Council for the Arts and for Research in the Social Sciences and Humanities.
The Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada is of course a funding body, which administers funds allocated to research, and awards bursaries. Created in 1977 to administer programs that were previously the responsibility of the Canada Council, it is directed by a 22-member council. Its budget for the 1991-92 fiscal year was $97,635,000, and it had 101 employees.
At the Department of External Affairs, about 25 people work international cultural and educational programs. The budget allocated to those programs for
1993-94 was in the neighbourhood of $27 million. The Canada Council, which was created in 1957, makes grants and services available to creative and performing artists and arts bodies. It has a staff of 248. Its programs are funded through revenue from an endowment fund, gifts, and parliamentary appropriations. Its budget for the 1991-92 fiscal year was $114 million. I wanted to situate all these important national bodies in their context.
The government has decided to put an end to the independence of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, to amalgamate it, so to speak, with the Canada Council. Has the government taken the trouble to explain the reasons for its decision to the members of this House?

which stems from this great program of fiscal restraint brought forward by the government in its February 25 budget which, as we know, was followed on December 2 by an additional statement announcing further decisions.
Included in those decisions was the winding up of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and a 10 per cent cut in the budget of many agencies and councils, including the Canada Council.
I have been unable so far to ascertain whether or not the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council will be affected by this new 10 per cent cut. I know that grants and awards will be affected. I know that the operations of many groups will have to adjust to these new fiscal restraints.

I would say, since they are two very distinct bodies, so very different from each other, that it will weaken the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and it will weaken this agency's contribution to Canada.
I refer to an article published by Robert Nadeau, the president of the Canadian Federation for the Humanities and a professor in the philosophy department of UQAM. I quote Professor Nadeau:
Unwarranted decision while it is certainly legitimate for a responsible government to want to reduce as much as possible the administration costs of the many programs and agencies it supports, it is not legitimate to proceed arbitrarily and without any explanation, as if the announced measure was self-evident and the people affected by such a measure had no right to be heard. February 16, 1993

I know that my time is up, but I just wanted to say in closing that the government has a lot of explaining to do. This budget of February 25, 1992 is full of such bad news that it is high time for this government to explain itself to Canadians. It is high time for this government to put its mandate to the Canadian people and to call an election to clarify this issue.

This legislation predominantly winds up a number of agencies, boards and commissions and moves their responsibilities to other offices. Generally speaking, I have no quarrel with that. While listening to my colleague, the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, speak earlier I was taken by the similarities that exist between Cape Breton and my own riding of Welland-St. Catharines- Thorold and the Niagara peninsula in general.
This piece of legislation is in 10 parts and I want to deal with the second and tenth parts. The second one deals with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. You might wonder why someone from southern Ontario would be talking about this particular aspect.
The government wants to close down the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and move its function and staff to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities agency. I
February 16, 1993

question how many jobs will be cut because of this and whether it will really be more efficient.
For this reason and on that basis I am opposed to this move to kill the ECBC, the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
The government stated in its budget speech that this and other organizations were being eliminated because: "They served their purpose and were no longer needed".
I believe this is wrong. I believe the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation is still needed today.
Witness some of these facts. The Cape Breton economy is still extremely troubled and special programs to address it are urgently needed now more than ever. The official unemployment rate reached almost 25 per cent earlier this year and now hovers around 23 per cent. The UI rate was only 16 per cent when the ECBC was created and Cape Breton's economy faces great challenges today just as it did in 1985.
The groundfishery is on the verge of collapse with huge quota cuts and job losses expected in 1993. Employment in the coal and steel industries is down. In my view the ECBC's job is not nearly complete.
Let us put that into juxtaposition with what is going on in the Niagara peninsula with regard to the unemployment patterns that have emerged in the last 18 to 24 months.
We in the Niagara peninsula have suffered the losses of well over 8,000 jobs in the last 18 months and if things go as they are projected to go, in the next 12 months we will be hovering around a loss of 10,000 jobs in the Niagara peninsula.
Last Saturday there was a demonstration by the members of the CAW of the Niagara peninsula who wanted to bring the plight of the people in our area to the attention of the governments of the day. Now we have an increase of almost 70 per cent in unemployment in the area.
Surely new programs are needed for the retraining of these people who incidentally are very highly skilled in the automotive industry, the steel industry and the abrasives industry. All these people are being affected. It

is not to say that these people want charity. They want recognition as there was in Cape Breton by the foundation of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the constituents of Hamilton West I consider it a privilege to rise on second reading debate of Bill C-93, an act to implement certain provisions of last year's budget, or as it is also known, an act to exterminate certain Crown agencies and appeal to disenfranchised Conservative supporters.
Like all eight budgets brought down by this government which slashed spending, cut away necessaiy resources and suppressed economic growth, the budget of February 25, 1992 was indeed no exception.
Since the government failed in those eight budgets to bring down the deficit which it promised to do when first elected, it decided to appear to be cost conscious and give the axe to several important Crown agencies.
With the government low in the polls and unable to control the deficit, as it has so prudently demonstrated, it decided to cut important public bodies and appealed to the notion that Canada had an over-bloated Public Service. By doing so it dealt Canada and important research and development a heavy blow.
Of course, this government has been fond of taking the Public Service to task and making a scapegoat out of it for years. Just ask the federal public servants in my riding of Hamilton West. Just ask members of the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety who are looking over their collective shoulders and expecting this government to terminate the centre. They fear that it might happen at any time.
When announcing the closures in this House, the Minister of Finance boasted of clearing the Public Service deck of over 500 public servants. He can boast that a large part of the department of immigration is going to relocate to Alberta. In fact, I stand to be corrected. It is going right into the riding of the Deputy Prime Minister who is the Minister of Finance is it not? I think it is.
Just ask the federal public servants in Hamilton West or in any riding what the workload is like at the immigration office in their particular ridings. I challenge any one of the members opposite. Have they ever taken a moment to go into the immigration office in their particular riding to see the paperwork that is stacked about a foot and a half high on the 14 desks that line the area inside that office? There are only seven, if you are lucky, federal public servants who are sitting and attempting and trying as best they can to keep ahead of the incredible workload at immigration while the cuts continue to happen.
Along the floor there are boxes of files. Heaven forbid that someone has called before you, fellow member, to inquire about that particular case. It has been pulled out of that particular box number 26 on the floor and set down on a desk somewhere. Your question has been responded to and then we have to call that immigration office on behalf of the constituent who is a little frustrated at the very least. Of course, they cannot find the file because it is out of box number 26 now and on someone's desk.
What about the savings from eliminating 46 public bodies or $22 million? Is it a lot of money? No, it is not a lot when Canada benefits so much from the work that the civil servants have done. It is not a lot when compared to the tens of millions of dollars the government paid out in consulting and advertising contracts. It is not a lot when compared to the $4.4 billion for the new Cadillac version of helicopters. We could have taken some pretty good advice to upgrade the existing ones.
The Law Reform Commission, which played a nonpartisan role-as all of these agencies have done-in providing information and research to the government and to Canadians, made several recommendations to the federal government on reforms to criminal law. Instead,
February 16, 1993

it chose to refer research to the Department of Justice where, practically speaking, it is vetted of contentious issues before it reaches the minister.
The Science Council of Canada is to be wound up. Since 1966 the federal government has relied upon valuable information and research on many areas of public policy.
The Economic Council of Canada, created in 1963, served Canada for three decades. It is closed. It is another important agency and contributor of important information that was given the axe.
In a report entitled Pulling Together the council explains how Canada's share of world trade has fallen. The prices of Canada's natural resources have been weak. Canada has higher manufacturing costs due to inflation and slower productivity.
In another report entitled A Lot to Learn the Economic Council of Canada noted that education is the key to the kind of jobs and the economic base that Canada will require in the future. Some of the recommendations include: by the year 2000 all 16-year old Canadians will be functionally literate; the proportion of high school graduates will be increased; science will be emphasized in high schools and the quality and quantity of high-tech training will be increased.
To learn some of the exact things that the Economic Council of Canada recommended in one report it cost taxpayers the same amount the government will save by closing more than over 30 agencies when it used more than $20 million of taxpayers' money to fund the so-called prosperity initiative.

The member for Hamilton West really put it the way it is. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you noted that as well. He really got to the centre of the issue. The centre of the issue is that this government has its priorities messed up. I am putting it kindly here because I am not sure that the word I want to use is parliamentary.
The member for Hamilton West pointed out that the government wants to save money-so it says-but it has provided no proof at all that the merging of the Canada Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council is going to save any money. It has not proven that the collapsing of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is going to save any money. There are no studies to back it up either. Also, it has not shown that that the effective closure of yet another government organization, Emergency Preparedness Canada, is going to save any money either.
Emergency Preparedness Canada is a rather interesting case. The member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke brought to our attention only a few weeks ago that the government actually announced the construction of a new facility in his riding in the election campaign of

1988 to house Emergency Preparedness Canada. It was around the community of Amprior if my memory serves me right.
Then the government allowed this thing to drag on and on. If my memory serves me right, it announced the construction of the building twice. Now you might think there are in fact two buildings there, but no. There is in fact no building at all or no new structure as was initially proposed. Nothing is there. That is the Prime Minister's version of the truth.
No, that is not what Canadians expect of the government. They expect a more ethical behaviour as it pertains to the awarding of government contracts, to the way it administers dollars, and more particularly to claiming there are alleged savings that are necessary in Bill C-93.
The government has not proven to me at all that these savings will be made. Even if the savings were there, why did it not cut out some of those generous untendered contracts it is giving to friends of the government instead? Why is the government not attacking the issue that way? Even if the government had exhausted all of those, even if the government had totally cleaned up its act, which it has not done, there is still the fundamental question. Even if we did want to, and I do not think we do, merge the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council with another agency, why merge it with the arts council? Why not merge it with another council?
February 16, 1993

What studies were done to determine if that is the best merger that could occur versus another one? None.

My party, my colleagues and I intend to vote against this bill. Of course, we still have a lot to say and we do not intend to let things go ahead so quickly. We here in this House all intend to try once again to make the Conservatives opposite, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, all his colleagues, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau, understand that this bill is wrong, particularly the clauses affecting the Canada Council as well as other agencies, especially Emergency Preparedness Canada and a number of other agencies.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise again to speak on this bill because I think Canadians are getting the impression very strongly that this government does not know what it is doing.
I do not know if it is devoid of ideas or if it has so little belief in the role of government in a civilized society that it really does not want to govern and does not believe

that government can or should function for the common good of all citizens.
We have ample evidence of the incompetence of this government, its lack of direction, its lack of understanding of what needs to be done to pull the country together and to set a clear course for the future. It is totally missing.
We have a bill that dismantles 10 agencies with no rationale, no analysis of how the functions of these agencies will be fulfilled in the future, or whether they should be abandoned, whether they can be done in a different way, or whether abandoning these agencies is going to cost money or save money. This is only one in a series of measures by government to destroy a number of agencies that have served this country well, to in fact carry on a mission based purely on ideology, not on common sense and good budgeting, to carry on an agenda of tearing down those things which Canadians regard as part of their heritage and as part of the foundation of this country.
We have seen it with the destruction of VIA Rail, the cutbacks to the CBC, with a number of actions geared more to simply getting rid of this and getting rid of that, with no sense of strengthening, no sense of serving Canadians better, no sense of ensuring that there is the objective qualified advice that a government needs to make sure that it is doing what is best for this country.
We have seen the loss of the Economic Council of Canada, the Science Council and the Pay Research Bureau which helped make for smoother labour negotiations in both the public and private sector. We have seen the transfer of patent development away from a corporation that was doing a fine job in that field into departments all across government at much greater cost and at much less benefit to the country.
If we have been insistent in our speeches, good. This is a bad bill when it comes forward with absolutely no justification based on the functions these agencies perform, absolutely no justification based on cost. It is because we have seen the results when this government has dismantled organizations with no clear sense of their purpose, no clear sense of the public importance of the

February 16, 1993

work they do and no clear sense of how they are going to replace that work.
We see as well this trend in the kind of budgeting we have had and the absolutely stupid determination to tax Canadians more, to provide them with a lesser level of services, to live budget after budget for eight years on the pretence that somehow this is going to put us in a sounder economic situation when in fact it has done exactly the opposite.
Canadians can add. They know that the debt this country was carrying eight years ago was barely one-third of what it is today. They know that the deficit they were carrying was much smaller than they are carrying today. They know that money was being spent then to provide services that Canadians needed, not being spent as it is now just to pay the interest on the debt.
I could address the individual agencies in this bill. Some of it we happen to agree with. We feel that some agencies outlive their purpose and function, but one does not simply say cut 10 per cent across government, cut staff to serve Canadians, cut agencies. One brings forward reasonable, sensible, well founded arguments as to why an agency has outlived its purpose and what cost savings there will be in replacing it with something else, or just simply abandoning it altogether.
The kind of blanket panic of just cutting here and cutting there shows an absolute lack of any sense of management, any sense of direction, any sense of responsibility to the taxpayers for public policy or for the management of their financial resources.
We see the results. We see the results when we read today that Canada may very well have trouble borrowing on the international markets in a very short period of time. This is the kind of legacy that this government has left us.
It is the result not of what is in this bill but of the fact that this bill is so typical of how this government has operated.
There is no sense of direction for the future. There is no sense of the purpose of government and the role it plays in the national life. There is no sense that we need a good and solid public sector in this country to work in partnership with the private sector, labour, educators, the provinces and people in their own communities if we want to address the problems of Canada and create the best possible future.
We oppose this bill. We oppose it because it is so typical of the running hither and yon, the crying about the sky is falling in, the total failure of the government to take its responsibilities as a government seriously and to provide the leadership that this country so desperately needs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate today.
The bill that is before the House now is intended, according to the government, to streamline the government, the efficiencies of the government. It is to make the running of government more efficient and to make the spending of the government go further.
That is a laudable goal and it is very commendable. The problem is that the government oftentimes has gone around with these bills and these proposals in a fashion that quite frankly is not beneficial to the people of this country.
I point out, for example, in this particular bill that the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council has been merged with Canada Council, which has caused no end of concern to these groups which are saying that this body was doing a very good job on its own. Merging them is only going to hurt the work that these people are doing.
This has happened in other areas. Last year the government in its same effort to streamline and cut costs cut the Law Reform Commission. It cut the Court Challenges Program. Both were very effective. Both made large contributions to this society. The Law Reform Commission in its work attempted to provide answers and suggestions as to the way we can better govern ourselves in this country.
That commission was cut at a time when we are facing an issue in this country of law and order. The media is carrying stories of crimes that are taking place in this country. They are of concern to people. There is the release of inmates who are considered to be dangerous criminals. There is a whole host of areas that the Canadian public is concerned about and is demanding answers to.
It is certainly going to be an issue in the next election. In fact, it is an issue right now. The Law Reform Commission was there to provide answers and did provide a lot of answers and suggestions. It is no longer there.
February 16, 1993

This whole area of crime prevention, reform of the Criminal Code and so on demands to be addressed right now. I think one of the things we have to look at is crime prevention. Certainly groups like the Law Reform Commission made comments on that. The justice committee right now is going to report on this.
It is very clear that Canada desperately needs a crime prevention strategy that is going to battle the social causes of crime right across this country. That is not a New Democratic position though. It sounds like one and it is one but that is not what the New Democrats alone are saying.
This is going to be the recommendation of the justice committee and the justice committee is made up of members from all sides of the House. The majority will be Tories, then Liberals and then New Democrats. That committee has heard evidence from so many areas and from such a wide range of witnesses that its members have been forced to come to that conclusion. I want to quote from one of the witnesses who came to this committee from Saskatoon, Sergeant Don Evers who stated: "Just as cancer eats away at people, crime eats away at our communities and societies. If we do nothing about it, it will continue to grow and erode everything".
Canada is the second most violent country of the Group of Seven nations, right behind the United States. Yet we have people in this country talking about building more jails, making tougher laws and becoming more confrontational.
There are areas where we do need tougher laws. That is true. This idea of having a confrontational approach simply does not work. The fact that we are starting to realize that is quite clear from the comments of the chair of that committee who, quoting from the newspaper, said: "If anyone had told me when I became an MP nine years ago that I'd be looking at the social causes of crime, I'd have told them they were nuts", said the P.C. member for Mississauga West who by the way is a former mountie. "I would have said lock them up for life and throw away the key, but not any more".
What about some of the Liberal members? The Liberal justice critic and member for Scarborough West
Government Orders
said in an interview: "There are definitely people who will continue to commit crimes no matter what you did for them, but there are many others who turn to crime because they have low self-esteem brought about by not having a job, the breakdown of their family or some other social condition".
It is very clear a whole new approach to the way we deal with the justice system is needed and in order to deal with that we need all the tools we can possibly avail ourselves of. Certainly the Law Reform Commission was a very important tool. That commission no longer exists. We simply have to look to other areas and there are other areas.
If a government is going to be committed to reforming the justice system, it makes very little sense to cut the Law Reform Commission and the Court Challenges Program. To take a case to the Supreme Court of Canada is extremely expensive. Unless there is a fund available for Canadians they are going to be unable to access the highest court in the land, even though they may have a very good issue.
This all-party committee is going to look at "Fighting Crime By Getting Through to the Social Causes", which is a very worthwhile document. I am very much looking forward to reading it. As a member of a subcommittee of justice which is looking at recodification of the Criminal Code, we will be tabling a report next week in the House as well.
I am glad to see that through this bill and other legislation the government is attempting to reorganize the way we do business in this country and save money. The problem is it is doing it in a fashion that is not beneficial to Canadians, particularly those in the lower income brackets or from certain social classes.
I hope that we as Canadians and parliamentarians can come to deal with some of these issues in a more logical fashion. This bill deals with a whole host of groups that are going to be cut and I wanted to focus on the area of justice because I think it demands attention right now. Certainly voters in the next election are going to be asking where the particular parties and candidates stand with respect to justice and law reform.

February 16, 1993
Government Orders
I think the answer is very clear, certainly from this member. If we are going to have law reform, its objective has to be to provide as safe a community as possible for all Canadians.
We can do that without building more jails and without being more confrontational. We also have to be sympathetic to the causes of crime and look at crime prevention as the main goal in creating a justice system in this country that is going to benefit all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-93 as it goes to third reading because this bill implements the parts of the 1992 federal budget.
Many of the sections of this bill are really designed for political purposes in the province of Alberta where the Reform Party last year at this time was doing quite well in the Gallup polls. The government was keen to show to the electorate in Alberta, where the Reform Party was doing very well, that it could cut and slash.
It is doing away with a lot of agencies here. In fact, most of them are just sort of moving over so the civil servants who were working before under the authority of an agency or board are taken back into the department. For instance, in the Department of Agriculture, products aboard is being done by the same government officials who are now acting within the Department of Agriculture, rather the Agriculture Products Marketing Board.
The Petroleum Monitoring Agency is useful because it tells Canadians how much they are paying in terms of excise tax and sales tax on petroleum products; how much is being charged by the retailer; how much is being charged by the various upstream sectors; the value of crude oil; the value of refining; the cost of distribution and so on.
Those sectors of the Petroleum Monitoring Agency are being taken back into the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It is mostly political matters that are being looked after in this whole bill rather than anything of any real substance.
The Prime Minister is concerned that when he goes to Alberta he can say he slashed and cut out government agencies. That is supposed to impress the electorate so it will vote for the Tories rather than the Reform Party which is doing quite well.
What has happened of course is that the Reform Party has gone into a complete decline. The question is whether the government would even have bothered with this legislation if it had known how much the Reform Party was going to slip in the most recent Gallup polls or in the polls that were done for Angus Reid.
I really want to talk about the budget, the government's general fiscal and monetary policy and its attitude toward the regions of this country. One of the sections for instance deals with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the changes being proposed there.
Many areas of the country have similar agencies. Southern Ontario and Quebec have the Ministry of Science, Technology and Trade. Northern Ontario has FEDNOR, the western provinces have their little agency while southern Ontario and the province of Quebec have the full department.
Those departments were designed to create economic opportunity and diversification. They have been singularly unsuccessful in diversifying the economy, not because of the agencies themselves doing their assigned tasks, which in the case of FEDNOR is really designed for quite small projects, at least in rural areas, but because of the government's over-all fiscal and monetary policy and general policy toward the regions of the country. Of course that is identified in the budget of 1992.
If we look at the Algoma district we see economic carnage because the government has essentially withdrawn from the problems.
If we look at the free trade deal of 1988, the government was saying it would solve the problems of the steel industry in cities like Sault Ste. Marie. Algoma Steel would not have to worry any more about countervail duties or dumping duties. The marketplace of the whole of North America would be open and the trade problems and restrictions that had been proposed in 1982 and 1986 would be over.
If you look at that community today Algoma Steel has essentially gone into ownership by the employees. It is a kind of receivership situation. How do we see the government's trade policy? It would be hard to describe it as anything but a disaster. After the 1988 free trade agreement was put in place the screws were put on by the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the monetary policy was very restrictive.
February 16, 1993

In 1989 and the first part of 1990 the Governor of the Bank of Canada imposed interest rates that were at least 5 to 6 percentage points above those in the United States. This drove the value of the Canadian dollar from 70 cents to 85 cents and even higher. We had the worst of all worlds. We had a very high dollar.
Companies like Algoma Steel were trying to produce steel with interest rates at 14 or 15 per cent while their American counterparts were paying 7 or 8 per cent interest. At the same time the dollar had appreciated by 12 or 14 percent. It was the worst of all worlds in a supposedly free trade area of North America.
If that was not bad enough, that kind of monetary policy gave the American producers a great opportunity. They immediately started to increase their exports to Canada by some 25 per cent, taking away markets for the Canadian steel industry. That industry was in total torment because of that.
It is not only those policies that have driven companies like Algoma Steel into receivership and employee ownership hoping to recover from that. In the past few weeks the United States government has imposed a dumping duty on the Canadian steel industry right across the board along with other countries.
Supposedly the free trade deal was going to resolve those problems. In fact it is much worse. The Americans have not backed down one iota and are not only imposing dumping duties, they are taking up a larger share of the Canadian market. The industry is in the most difficult time in its history.
This budget bill, Bill C-93, an implementation act that we are debating today is being brought in at a time when the government's fiscal and monetary policies are extremely Draconian for the Canadian steel industry. That industry today is in a terrible turmoil. It is during a time when there should have been an agreement.
We talked back in the 1960s, 1970s and early 1980s of a North American steel agreement, something like the Canada-U.S. automobile agreement. That agreement is being proposed again in spite of the fact that we have a FIA, but the Americans are not agreeing to it. We are in a free trade area where there is really no free trade. All you get is countervail duties, anti-dumping duties and a
Government Orders
demand for more and more of the Canadian marketplace which just ultimately costs more and more Canadian jobs. That really came out of that budget.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand here today to speak on Bill C-93, which is a budget implementation bill and in effect dissolves many agencies and merges others.
In some of the cases the agencies should be dissolved. They have not been used. They have not been of use for some time. Indeed, one would wonder why it has not been considered before.
However, in other cases we wonder why the government is behaving in this fashion. It appears there was absolutely no consultation. In some cases the government may say it was due to fiscal restraint. We acknowledge this is a terribly difficult time economically for all of us. Perhaps there is reason to consider fiscal restraints. However, after looking deeper into some of these mergers it is realized that perhaps in some cases it will not only not save dollars but may also cost even more.
One of the things we would like to see when this bill goes to committee is that there be extensive consultation with some of the agencies that are suggested to be merged.
Perhaps when I was first elected I was quite naive in thinking that there was a lot of co-operation and consultation before a budget measure was implemented. However, shortly after I was elected I was made an associate critic in one of the fields and had been closely following the speeches made by the minister in charge of the particular department. If I can recall this was in February of 1989, but in any case it was the first budget I was here for.
It just so happened that approximately one week before the budget was read the minister in question went out west and gave a speech. He told the people concerned that if there were to be any way that the particular program would be discontinued they would be given ample opportunity, ample notice but that it would not be discontinued at the time.

February 16, 1993
Government Orders
Lo and behold, one week later in the budget the program was cut off as of midnight that night. It surprised me somewhat. I thought: Well is the gentleman not a minister? Is he not a part of what happens with the pre-budget deliberations? Elow could he make a speech out west guaranteeing consultation and plenty of advance warning and have one week or so later the Minister of Finance actually make him look like a bit of a fool because the program was cut off with no grace period of six months and so on.
I asked the minister: "Did they not speak to you before?" He just shrugged his shoulders and walked away. I thought that was not the way to do budgeting. When doing a budget, the departments are brought in to try to find the best way to utilize the dollars available. Yes, cutbacks are extremely difficult and sometimes are necessary.
I have worked as an accountant. I know how easy it is to look at an amount and think that it can be done without. But many times there would be easier ways and perhaps ways of saving even more money while doing the work that we are doing. Sometimes just looking at a sheet of paper and knocking off numbers is costlier than the amount of money it saves.
I ask this government to please reconsider and when the legislative committee is formed and studies this bill that we allow extensive consultations, especially when we deal with part II and part III of this bill which deal with the Canada Council for the Arts and Research in the Social Sciences and Humanities.
Part III of the legislation winds up the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and transfers its functions and staff to the Canada Council. Certain functions and staff of the Department of External Affairs and International Trade that deal with the promotion of Canadian culture abroad would also be transferred to the Canada Council. I am sure there will be some very good suggestions made by people who are involved in these councils who know the good that is being done and the ways by which the councils could be used more advantageously without costing the government a great deal of money. It is absolutely essential when we streamline that we do not, contrary to the spirit of the legislation, cause more cost for the taxpayer.
The new Canada Council would have to develop a whole new international division and network quite apart from its domestic concerns if it is to administer the various cultural programs effectively. That has not been part of its mandate at this time. We are asking that the Canada Council perform this function. Maybe the Canada Council would like to have this function. Perhaps we could allow that function to be carried on by external affairs as it has been up until now.
As well, staff in various posts abroad would now be accountable to two masters, that is, the Canada Council and the heads of the posts. How would that save money? It is far better to have them answerable to only one boss. Again, we ask that amendments which would facilitate this be considered.
It is a matter of being humane in the cutbacks. It is a matter of using your head and as well as cutting back, doing the best that you can do. The only way we can properly run this country and offer the kinds of programs we need and at the same time manage to better spend taxpayers' dollars is to have all people work together. We cannot have only one person unilaterally cut back at one level just perhaps to cost more at another level. That is not the way we will address the deficit position we are in, or for that matter the deficit positions of other levels of government and other departments.
We are asking that this government stop this unilateral decree in terms of budgets. I do want to stress it is extremely important we allow every due consideration. Those agencies that should be closed down by all means if they are not in use now let us get it over with and close them down. Those agencies that are performing very valuable functions should be separated and allowed to continue to provide the kinds of services that they have in the past so that they can continue to make us a great and wonderful country. It is absolutely essential and I beseech this government not to continue in decreeing budget cuts but to consult and together we can make it work.
