speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Skelly (North Island-Powell River) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should cancel the proposal to amalgamate the RCMP Public Complaints Commission with the RCMP External Review Committee, and furthermore the government should implement the recommendations contained in the 1990-91 RCMP Public Complaints Commission Annual Report.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today I would like to propose that we change the direction in which the government is moving in one particular case. This is the case of amalgamating two very worth-while agencies: the RCMP External Review Committee and the RCMP Public Complaints Commission.
The concerns I have involve an incident that happened in Gibsons, British Columbia, on September 30, 1988. On that particular night an individual happened to be under the influence of alcohol and sleeping in a local pub. The owners asked that the individual be removed. The individual was then subsequently taken to the RCMP station and throughout the night an altercation resulted.
Private Members' Business
The individual was taken out of the RCMP cells during the night. He was subjected to the exercise of force by a police officer involved. There had been an altercation in the cells as well. Later on in the course of the night the individuals who were in the cell began to ask that the person be dealt with by a physician. It was clear that the person was badly injured. It was not exactly clear how those injuries came about, but very definitely throughout the night the individual did not have access to medical attention.
The next morning there were no charges taken and suddenly all the other individuals in the cell were asked to leave. This individual was held back to account for a parking ticket in Sechelt, British Columbia. Then, once his brother dealt with the parking ticket in another community, he was released out into the street where he promptly could not function because of his physical condition.
A taxicab picked him up and took him to the hospital. The hospital examined him and my understanding of the injuries were that his face had been stoved in, his ribs broken and his spleen had been ruptured. He was in fact in danger of dying. The hospital picked him up by helicopter and took him to North Vancouver to deal with the injuries.
The two points the commission findings dealt with were an improper procedure on the part of the RCMP officers involved and failure to provide medical attention. Had it not been for the RCMP Public Complaints Commission, this would never have seen the light of day.
There were definitely attempts by RCMP officers involved to obstruct the process of this complaint. It was extremely difficult to deal with it. In any other agency, such as the provincial ombudsman, nobody would have essentially picked this complaint up. It is ironic that the RCMP Public Complaints Commission came into force at midnight, October 1. Even though this had occurred on September 30, I gather the RCMP took the commission to court arguing that since the event had commenced prior to the proclamation and imposition of this legislation it did not have jurisdiction.
The Federal Court upheld that jurisdiction and the case went ahead. It took years. Eventually the RCMP admitted wrongdoing, apologized for the event and then wound up in an out of court settlement resolving it years later.

February 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
The point is not to criticize the RCMP. The RCMP is the finest police force that one can point to in Canada if not in the world. It is absolutely critical that the force maintain high morale and that the complaints commission not be used as an instrument to harass the police force when it is carrying out the will of the public so that fair, even-handed and effective law enforcement takes place.
We are concerned about the odd incident, the odd individual who is not suited to the rigours of police work. There must be a mechanism by which the complaints of the public can be brought before a commission or an agency that handles these fairly.
I would like to read the mandate of the External Review Committee. It says: "The RCMP External Review Committee was created to provide an independent, impartial recommendation to the commissioner on grievances, formal discipline, discharge and demotion under the provisions of the RCMP Act. Any case resulting in a formal discipline, discharge and demotion is referred to the committee by the Commissioner of the RCMP unless the member requests that it proceeds otherwise".
This is a totally different matter. It is almost a committee that handles labour grievances within the police force. I think it is an extremely valuable, useful and productive arrangement where officers within the police force can ask that these complaints be dealt with within a more impartial purview than with members of the RCMP.
On the other hand, the principles laid out in the RCMP Public Complaints Commission are different. It talks about two important functions: that the mandate of the Public Complaints Commission is to provide individual members of the public with an effective mechanism that they can make complaints in. The public also, in laying complaints, must not interfere with the public's interest in the fair and proper enforcement of the law. It is a very delicate balance. It is not there to disrupt the process of fair and even-handed law enforcement, but it is also there to deal in a fair and equitable way with the complaints of the public.
A number of important principles have to be looked at. We cannot allow these two agencies to be melded together. It is a blurring of their purposes.
The public is already sceptical enough, when you say RCMP public complaints, that it is an agency of the RCMP and that it works hand in glove with the people against whom they have a complaint. That is not true.
The first principle we should be looking at is that police forces have strict accountability in the use of force, especially the use of deadly force, which we have been encountering lately in a great many public complaints, not against the RCMP but other police forces. There is a strict accountability of the use of force against members of the public.
The second principle is that the complaints have a fair and impartial investigation mechanism to ensure the public that they are fully investigated and they know the consequences and outcome.
The third principle is that the public be aware of the process. When you talk to members of the general public it is ironic that they do not have any idea that this organization exists. Many people who have complaints against the RCMP say: "There is nothing you can do. This is the force of the state and if you wind up complaining against them the force will come down on you even harder". There is an element of truth in this.
I think there have been at least a dozen complaints against police actions in the community of Gibsons. It is interesting, when individuals were charged and the use of force was involved in the laying of that charge, the individuals who laid the complaint about what they felt was the inappropriate use of force, usually a month later or some time later, even further charges emerged. So there was a real deterrent against the individual making a complaint and it was recommended often by friends not to complain because they would make it even worse.
However, the public must be aware that there is a process by which they can get to an agency that will investigate their complaints.
When we went to the hospital in this community and asked if the records showed that when individuals were brought into this hospital that they complained about the excessive use of force or injury because of excessive force of the RCMP. It never appeared in the hospital emergency records and it was not traceable back through hospital records, so it is extremely difficult.
It is my understanding that this is now changed. If an individual comes in and says how he or she has been injured, the hospital will at least record that the injury
February 16, 1993

was as a result of police force action and the use of force in the law enforcement process.
The public is not aware of this organization. I think it is important that all referral agencies and hospitals should make it clear where one can get a fair and equitable hearing of one's complaint, a thorough investigation.
The RCMP must co-operate with an investigatory commission and that co-operation must be seen to get to the bottom of a complaint. In many cases the RCMP officer has been found to be completely justified in the use of force for the protection of himself, protection of others and for the public good of enforcing the law.
In other cases, there was a misunderstanding and an explanation to the complainant about what the procedures are has often satisfied people. There has often been a simple apology that in the heat of the moment measures might have been used that were precautionary. Then in a very small number of cases there is in fact a legitimate concern and a good thorough investigation is useful in clearing the air and resolving the matter for future police operations procedure.
This procedure, with RCMP co-operation, gets to the bottom of what its members are doing. Getting to the bottom of what its members are doing can change police operations and make our police force a more effective agency, more highly regarded in the eyes of the public for doing the work of the public.
It is absolutely critical that this process be transparent. If in those small number of cases where an individual requires discipline, where changes are made as a result of a complaint of improper procedure, then it is incumbent upon the RCMP to let the complainant know what the outcome was.
At this time, there is no indication of what occurs. The commissioner of the RCMP in responding to the report and recommendations of the commission in a finding is not required to produce that information to the complainant.
I do not know how we got to the point of talking about the recommendations in the 1990-91 report. I believe what we are talking about is the recommendations in the
Private Members' Business
1989-90 report. Substantial recommendations were put forward for changes in the RCMP legislation. Not only do these agencies have to be held apart in order to keep and encourage the public confidence in an organization that is there to handle complaints, but the legislation has to be strengthened to make it more effective.
It is interesting that in asking to be able to distribute interim reports and final reports of the agency, they are asking for the authority to make these matters of the public record and that the public can refer to previous actions taken by the commission in the event of certain kinds of activities. There is no reason that this should not be a matter of public record. There is no reason that this recommendation should not be implemented.
Another thing is that the commissioner within 60 days should be required to provide notice to the commission and to the complainant of the commissioner's response to the report and recommendation of the commission. The complainant, as I mentioned before, is entitled to know what kind of action is to be taken in a case where there was inappropriate use of force or inappropriate action on the part of the police force and its members. That should be reported. Any disciplinary action, any changes taken, should be reported back to the complainant and the commission.
The commission asks for the ability to share information that it has gathered, even personal information with the provinces who are responsible for contracting for those police forces. It is important that the attorneys general of the various provinces have access to the kinds of information that may in future affect important police operation matters. It would allow them to co-ordinate and to change actions of other police forces where it is important. This kind of change to the legislation would certainly help and be effective.
An interesting problem arose if the complaint is made against the police force in its entirety as well as against a member of the police force. It is suggested in the recommendation that if it is simply against a member, the discipline falls on the member. The member becomes a scapegoat and the force is held blameless. The entire operation of the police force is not up for

February 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
consideration. It is absolutely important that this recommendation be implemented as well.
The commission in its recommendations in the 1989-90 report asked for a mechanism to be provided to permit mediation of complaints where the police force and the complainant could sit down in a mediated situation rather than going to court and rather than being placed in a continuous adversarial, confrontational type of arrangement that that environment provides. Mediation as an opportunity should be provided.
In summation, it is important that those recommendations be considered seriously. There should be ongoing dialogue between the office of the Solicitor General and the chairperson of this commission for the implementation of those recommendations. We could have an improved legislative base from which this commission could operate. It would be an agency that is more effective in resolving the complaints of the public.
In fact in the long run this will enhance the credibility of Canada's police force and will improve the law enforcement activities in Canada.
One of the requirements that we should be looking for in this House is a statement from the Solicitor General. That will probably be the subject of the next private member's motion. The subject of the next private members' motion is probably that the Solicitor General report to this House the progress on the implementation of these particular recommendations.
It is important that this agency not be rolled into the External Review Committee, that its mandate and its responsibility be blurred by an activity which is not in any way related.
The suggestion is that the government will save money in this process. By the time the moves are all made and the two agencies move into their new facilities, expand the number of floors they take up and rearrange things no money will be saved. In the long run, it is likely that RCMP Public Complaints Commission will be harmed in its ability to carry out its absolutely critical tasks.
Hopefully the government is in a position to reconsider what I think is a strategic error in the law enforcement policy of Canada. To reiterate, the RCMP is literally the finest police force in the country, if not in the entire
world. It is respected from coast to coast to coast by all Canadians as having done an enormously good job. When there have been complaints, we have seen those complaints addressed and we have moved on.
At this point there has to be serious consideration by the government to complaints from the public, that those complaints be moved on quickly and effectively, without harming law enforcement and to the satisfaction of the complainant. At least they got a fair hearing.
The RCMP sets a standard for law enforcement in this country. The handling of complaints in an effective, fair, even-handed manner where the complainant gets to know the reasons a situation occurred, for better or for worse does not harm this police force. It does not harm the cause of law enforcement. At least it lays to rest the often serious concerns of complainants.
It also sets an example to other police forces in this country that there is strict accountability, that the RCMP has the courage and the integrity to answer. It has full accountability to the citizens' confidence in it of delegating the right to use force in the enforcement of the laws. That example would go a long way to resolving many of the complaints that we are faced with each day.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise today to address the House on a motion sponsored by the hon. member for North Island-Powell River, which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should cancel the proposal to amalgamate the RCMP Public Complaints Commission with the RCMP External Review Committee, and furthermore the government should implement the recommendations contained in the 1990-91 -
Or rather the 1989-90, as my colleague corrected in his presentation
-RCMP Public Complaints Commission Annual Report.
From the outset, it must be understood that the issue of the consolidation of the RCMP Public Complaints Commission and the RCMP External Review Committee is separate from the proposal to consider amending the RCMP Act for the purpose of improving the complaints process.
February 16, 1993

The former action is structural, a streamlining of the system to improve efficiency.
The latter pertains to a substantive review of the effectiveness of the accountability mechanism, and is in no way precluded by a merger of the two agencies.
To better explain this distinction, let me first provide a brief history of the creation of the Public Complaints Commission and the External Review Committee.
Many significant amendments to the RCMP Act were passed in 1986. Within this package of amendments, a substantial number, including the creation of the RCMP Public Complaints Commission and the RCMP External Review Committee, were in direct response to the findings and recommendations of the Marin commission of inquiry, embodied in the commission's report of 1976.
The Marin commission was established in 1974 to inquire into public complaints, internal discipline and grievance procedure within the RCMP.
The Marin commission recommended that within the RCMP, the public complaint system operate separately from the disciplinary system. However, at the independent review stage, the commission recommended the appointment of a sole authority, referred to in the report as the federal police ombudsman, to review and make recommendations on matters of public accountability, internal discipline and grievances.
Notwithstanding the recommendation for a single review authority, two separate agencies were formed through amendments to the RCMP Act in 1986: the RCMP Public Complaints Commission to review RCMP handling of complaints made against individual members of the force by the public and the RCMP External Review Committee to review and make recommendations on certain types of grievances initiated by members and appeals of formal discipline and discharge or demotion actions initiated by management.
The committee became operational in 1986 and the commission in 1988.
It is important to keep in mind that ten years passed from the time the Marin commission submitted its report of recommendations in 1976 until the RCMP Act was amended.
In that period of time successive governments researched, consulted on, and refined the issues that
Private Members' Business
resulted in significant amendments to the RCMP Act and the creation of two civilian oversight bodies. Compare this deliberate and extensive process of consideration with the fact that, after only two years of the commission's being operational, the then Chairman proposed in the 1989-90 annual report 30 recommendations for improvement necessitating further substantial amendments to the RCMP Act.
As I have stated, the first study was an extensive process that evolved during a period of more than 12 years, which included the two-year inquiry by the Marin Commission. The Public Complaints commission recommendations were based on a review of only two years of operational experience.
The recommendations in the 1989-90 Public Complaints Commission annual report touch on the scope and nature of the complaint process, post-complaint discipline and the monitoring of the complaint process.
As I indicated, changes to the RCMP public complaint process would necessitate further amendments to the RCMP Act.
Because the commission had only been in operation for two years, it was believed premature to consider amendments to the RCMP Act at that time.
As part of the streamlining measures contained in the government's February 1992 budget, it was announced that a number of agencies would be consolidated, including the RCMP Public Complaints Commission and the RCMP External Review Committee. This was done to provide a more efficient management process to handle complaint investigations and grievances.
The purpose of the amalgamation is to reduce administrative costs, increase efficiencies in program delivery and avoid duplication.
Bill C-93, an act to implement certain government organization provisions of the budget tabled in the House of Commons on February 25, 1992, would create the new independent review commission for the RCMP. This bill was tabled in the House on February 5, 1993 and has just been passed on second reading and referred to a legislative committee. With the bill now before the House, my colleague from North Island-Powell River has the opportunity to propose amendments during the

February 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
committee's clause-by-clause proceedings or at report stage in the House of Commons.
The return to the original Marin commission recommendation of a single review authority does not detract from the distinctiveness of these two functions or impugn the impartiality of either process.
In practice, all the major activities of these two agencies will be assumed by the single agency. Moreover, as many of the administrative functions of the commission and the committee are analogous, the integration of these two agencies will result in greater efficiency and administrative savings. As well, once the new commission is established, there will be a reduction to one chairperson, one vice-chairperson and one deputy chairperson from the current configuration of, in total, two chairmen and two vice-chairmen.
With respect to the potential for conflict of interest, or real or apparent bias arising from one agency handling both public complaints and internal grievances and discipline, Bill C-93 deals with these issues. For example, one particular provision ensures that the deputy chairperson review any matter previously reviewed by the chairperson in the other context, and the legislation provides that the chairperson cannot use information that he or she has obtained from a discipline case to initiate a complaint in the public interest.
The legislation which will give effect to the new agency was drafted after a series of extensive consultations among officials of the Public Complaints Commission, the External Review Committee, the Privy Council Office, the RCMP and the Secretariat of the Ministry of the Solicitor General to ensure that all issues and potential difficulties were fully addressed.
In the end, we are maintaining an independent review system, resembling more closely the single authority envisaged by the Marin commission, with legislative safeguards that protect against possible conflict of interest situations and streamlined to increase efficiency and reduce administrative costs. The new body will continue to provide the same high quality of complaints investigation and grievance review.
I have explained why the recommendations of the 1989-90 Public Complaints Commission annual report
were not pursued. Once the independent review commission of the RCMP is established and running and there has been a sufficient period of experience with it, improvements might suggest themselves.
As the system has matured since the 1989 recommendations and because of the amalgamation, it would not be appropriate to base future recommendations on the 1989-90 review. After a sufficient time of operation, we will be able to consider whether it is necessary to take a fresh look at the system with the participation of the independent review commission, ministry officials, the RCMP, both rank and file and management, the Department of Justice and the central agencies.
The consolidation of the commission and the committee does not preclude a subsequent review of the efficacy of the legislation. This is not a situation where a choice has to be made to amalgamate or conversely to implement the recommendations embodied in the 1989-90 annual report.
The decision to amalgamate is premised on this government's commitment to implement streamlining measures. This consolidation in no way jeopardizes the integrity of the oversight mechanism which is ultimately established. If there are any problems or issues that arise after a reasonable period of operation, they can be addressed at the appropriate time.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am delighted to take part this evening in making some comments on this motion by the member for North Island-Powell River. May I begin by saying that the parliamentary secretary gives a very interesting and accurate historical perspective on what happened.
May I comment briefly on what I consider to be an incredible Dickensian coincidence in connection with this motion. I notice that the member has a motion dated March 30, 1992. It concerns the proposed amalgamation of the two bodies. He happens to have it on the Order Paper today, of all days. What a fluke, since we happen to be speaking today, of all days, on Bill C-93. One portion of Bill C-93 happens to be precisely the exact same subject matter that the hon. member brought up March 30, 1992. It has taken this long to get here.
February 16, 1993

I guess in effect he has had an extra kick at the can to criticize at least a portion of Bill C-93 after we just voted to have no further debate on Bill C-93 and to proceed to committee. By the way, I voted against that because we should not be stopping debate in this House of Commons.
However, having said that, let us take a look at what that portion of Bill C-93 attempts to accomplish and why the hon. member moved his motion. It is an attempt to consolidate the External Review Committee and the RCMP Public Complaints Commission. The plain and simple reason is to save money. We are told that if these two bodies are amalgamated, there will be a saving of approximately $1 million a year. In government language there will be a reduction of seven person-years in the operation of this new commission.
The hon. member who spoke just before me also indicated that there would only be one chairperson instead of two and one vice-chairperson instead of two, with the usual support mechanisms.
Contrary to popular belief and to the unfortunate slurs that have been foisted upon the Liberal Party by the government, we are not averse to saving money where that makes sense. We support saving money where it makes sense. We think in this particular instance that it makes some sense to amalgamate the two agencies.
It is interesting that the Conservative member opposite reminded us that at one time there was a feeling that these two commissions should be one. Notwithstanding that feeling, they became two. Now, for budgetary constraints it has been decided that they become one again.
Is there something wrong with that? The member for North Island-Powell River pointed to three specifics. I wrote them down. He wanted a fair and impartial investigation mechanism. That is reasonable. He did not, however, cite any evidence in his remarks as to why this proposed amalgamated commission would be anything but fair and impartial in its investigations. He said that the RCMP must co-operate with the commission. Who could disagree? However, is there any evidence that the RCMP would not co-operate with this proposed commission? Is there any evidence that as a matter of policy
Adjournment Debate
the RCMP has not been co-operating with both the External Review Committee and the RCMP Public Complaints Commission? I would suggest that there is no such evidence.
He said that that process must be transparent. By that of course he means that the public should be able to judge what is going on. That is something that is not going to be changed by amalgamating.
Am I almost out of time, Mr. Speaker? Let me finish. I want to bring to the attention of those who are listening who have followed this one specific clause of Bill C-93 as it deals with this independent complaint commission. I cite it specifically. Clause 25(6) reads:
No member of the force is eligible to be appointed or to continue as
a member of the commission.
There can be no question of independence since there cannot be a member of the force on the commission.
Unfortunately I do not have time to comment on the recommendations in the RCMP Public Complaints Commission annual report, particularly since the wrong date was given.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak about transportation. It arises out of a question that I put to the Minister of Transport on November 20, 1992. It was a question that was very pertinent to what is going on in Atlantic Canada and the lack of a transportation policy by this government.

February 16, 1993
Adjournment Debate
We were dealing with the situation in which CP had requested the abandonment of portions of the line from Saint John to Montreal. The effect of the abandonment of that line would mean the end of VIA Rail service three out of six days of the week.
We are seeing more and more pressure being put on the highway systems of Atlantic Canada. We realize, of course, that the railway has been abandoned in Newfoundland. It has been abandoned in Prince Edward Island. The government is in the process of abandoning the line from Truro to Sydney, all of which puts major burdens on our highway network. We are clearly facing a major problem in New Brunswick as well as in other provinces in Atlantic Canada, but the unique thing about Atlantic Canada is that all roads eventually go through New Brunswick if you are trying to travel from anywhere in Atlantic Canada to Upper Canada, as we call it, to Ontario or Quebec.
That means that when you tamper with a rail line and abandon that then that brings about greater pressure on our highways. Anybody who has been in New Brunswick realizes the major problem with truck transportation on a two-lane Trans-Canada Highway.
I asked the minister to tell us what the policy is. What is the transportation policy of this government as it relates to Atlantic Canada?
The answer comes back that they are looking at it, they are not sure, that all the lines have not yet really been abandoned, they will study it and they will get back to us.
Clearly there has to be a transportation policy which is going to be supportive of the three major elements of transportation in Atlantic Canada which are air, highway and rail.
If this government has its way there will be only one rail line that runs from Halifax to Montreal and if this government takes the next step, it will probably try to sell off that line to another private concern so that there will not be a national rail line that runs from Halifax to Vancouver. That is a shocking and callous display by this government.
My speaking time is limited and I have much on my mind and many concerns about this government's lack of policy in the area of transportation. Mr. Speaker, I can tell by the look on your face that you are concerned about it as well. It is a concern for all citizens of this country. We have to link this country together from east
to west. If we are going to have a disjointed transportation policy that puts danger on our highways and destroys the steel linkage across this nation, then in effect we have started the dismemberment of this country.
I ask the government to come forward with a policy, stop rail line abandonment until that policy is in place and do something about the Trans-Canada Highway in New Brunswick and all of Atlantic Canada. It needs an upgrading, it needs something done. Let us see some action from this government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the hon. member for Moncton who raised these issues of concern.
First, I would like to deal with the question of the rails because of course by issuing notices of intent, CP Limited has initiated the rail line abandonment regulatory process available under law.
There are certain real opportunities that should be considered by those interested in the continuation of rail service on these lines. The National Transportation Agency hearings will provide a perfect forum for all parties to raise their concerns.
With respect to highways, the federal government has certainly recognized that the road system in New Brunswick is in bad condition. A study of the national highway system identified that while only 961 kilometres or 4 per cent of the national highway system is in New Brunswick, over $2.2 billion or 16 per cent of the total required to upgrade the whole system is located in that province.
The government does not have to apologize for its commitment to highway spending in maritime Canada. New Brunswick is benefiting now from a cost-shared agreement which provided $131 million of federal funds over eight years to upgrade the highway system. For that matter since 1984 the federal government has contributed over $650 million in highway programs in Atlantic Canada alone, which represents a higher investment in this region than in any other region in Canada.
New Brunswick and Newfoundland have been the largest recipients of federal highway funds with over $240 million and $250 million contributed respectively.
In addition, the Minister of Finance announced in his December economic statement the national infrastructure program which will result in more than $2 billion during the next five years. Federal assistance will be provided on priority highway projects in New Brunswick
February 16, 1993

and Nova Scotia in order that significant work can be commenced on development of an Atlantic expressway.
We too are sorry that details have not yet been ironed out. I know that the Minister of Transport has made this a very real priority and that the message is clearly understood by the negotiators who are determined to strike the best deal possible for all parties concerned.

Mr. Speaker, this discussion started with a question that I asked of the minister of fisheries five months ago yesterday.
In response to a question I put to him, he said that because he entered into agreements with aboriginals for conservation purposes, for management of fish resources and for the sale of fish that there are tensions in the industry in B.C.
Those are not the reasons. Had they been agreements for conservation, everybody would have supported them. Agreements for management would have had the same degree of support. The only question with sale is how many? If the aboriginals were selling the number of fish that they were allotted, there would have been no problem with that either.
The problem is there is no policing of the regulations and to the extent that there was supervision, the supervision was not even-handed. Everyone knows and admits that now. DFO officials will admit they were told to observe, record and report but not to do anything further than that if they were dealing with aboriginals. With respect to others, they were to arrest them on the spot if they liked.
As a result of these tensions the minister said a great deal is being made of a situation of the alleged disappearance. It is much more than alleged. A DFO official told me that 1.2 million sockeye had gone missing. When Dr. Pearse did his study he came up with a figure closer to 500,000 but whatever, it is a lot of sockeye. It is not a little thing. It is something pretty important.
The minister said it was a great success, a great year for B.C., because so many more spawners returned in this low cycle year than were expected. With respect to
Adjournment Debate
the Stuart Lake run, perhaps the most important of all, while we were hoping and expecting and counting on getting 200,000 spawners, according to Dr. Pearse we got
64,000,	less than one-third of what we anticipated. We knew they were in the river, but they did not get to the spawning ground.
It is not just that they did not get there. The ones that arrived, according to Dr. Pearse, were all net scarred. They had fought a tough fight to get through the many nets that were in the Fraser River picking up these fish. The question remains, and we will not know for another four years, whether or not the spawning of even one-third of the expected number was successful. We will just have to wait and see.
It was a bad year in British Columbia. It is not because of the new strategy that there have been troubles. It is because the strategy was not applied even-handedly. It goes against both. We know that Indians were taking advantage of the situation and we know that whites were taking advantage as well.
Stories were related and not denied by anyone that white fishing boats would take a single Indian on board and put that person on deck where he or she could be seen. They then could do almost anything they wanted without fear of being picked up by DFO officials.
That is what makes it wrong. It was not even-handed. There was not the supervision that was needed to guarantee the resource. Those are the problems in the industry, not the fact that a new strategy has been introduced.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member opposite, who has shown real concern about what happened last summer in the fisheries on the west coast, yes there were problems. I will be the first to admit that. Also, as the summer unfolded, corrective action was taken to make sure that the fish that we wanted to get to the spawning grounds would get there.
We had estimated that there would be 6.4 million fish, which exceeded the pre-season estimates and the largest run of a low-cycle year in 80 years. Salmon every four

Adjournment Debate
years return to their birthplace, spawn and die. The cycle then starts all over again.
The number of early Stuart sockeye which returned to spawn, some 65,000-1 have seen 66,000, I have seen
64,000,	and I have seen 65,000, but within 1,000 of each other-has only once been surpassed since 1960. That I believe was four years previous.
Over all the British Columbia commercial fishing fleet had a very successful fishing season this year. In fact, it has been estimated that it had over 400,000 fish, more than what the total allotment should have been, but that is not the problem that the hon. member was alluding to. He is alluding to the problem of what took place on the lower Fraser River of the early Stuart runs.
When the problem was identified, and the member opposite will have to agree with this, on August 6 all native fishing was disallowed in the river and the nets were taken out. This was watched by helicopter surveillance so that all of the spawners, all the fish that were in the river to spawn, would get back to their grounds. A very successful season of spawners has been there, so we can look forward four years from now to a very successful fishing season.

Mr. Speaker, on September 17 I directed a question in the House to the acting Minister of Communications. It was with respect to the drama documentary The Valour and the Horror, produced by the National Film Board and shown on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
This piece of work is now being distributed by the National Film Board to schools and other institutions. The problem is that anyone can rent it and anyone who wants to rent it, gets it.
The film series is billed as a drama documentary, a documentary. Dramatized truth is what it is supposed to be.
The drama documentary that runs three parts is anything but truth. The level of historical rightness contained in the series is totally and completely false. There is a complete lack of balance and it pays no attention to the allied situation in World War II. It has an emphasis on the negative. It demonstrates Canadians as
inept, murderers and horror creators. It is a shameful expression by our National Film Board and by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Veterans right across Canada have risen up. They have written and complained but that does not matter. The McKenna brothers were out to get Sir Arthur Harris, chief of bomber command. He was shown as ruthless, a murderer and someone who would bomb and kill women and children.
The Normandy-Dieppe activity was shown as a case where Canadians were badly led. They were incompetent troops and untrained troops. They were troops that did not know what they were doing. In Hong Kong, where our troops held off the Japanese invaders for 18 days, one of our men received the Victoria Cross.
This documentary shows our troops as incompetent. This is the invention of the McKennas. They have decided to rewrite history. Forget about the truth. Forget about Adolf Hitler. Forget about the fact that the German war machine had taken over all of Europe, all of the European part of the Soviet Union and that it occupied North Africa.
Forget about the fact that the Japanese, who brutally treated people, had occupied all of southeast Asia. Forget about the damage done and say our people murdered a few people. They killed a few people. A few of the enemy civilians were bombed. That is the spirit that the McKennas want to give to national television.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the hon. member for Mississauga South.
The communications minister has always respected the autonomy principle regarding the activities of the National Film Board and does not interfere with the creativity aspect of its decisions. As a producer and distributor of films and video material, the NFB is entirely autonomous in creating and marketing its productions.
February 16, 1993

As you know, Mr. Speaker, The Valour and the Horror is a three-part documentary on Canada's participation in World War II produced by Galafilm Inc., of Montreal, in collaboration with the NFB and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This film was reviewed in minute detail during the public hearings conducted by the Senate sub-committee on veterans affairs following numerous complaints from some veterans and military historians who claimed that this film gave a distorted account of World War II events.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief four minutes I have allotted to me I wish to expand on a question that I asked one week ago.
On that day, February 9, an event occurred in the legal history of Canada which is unprecedented. The coroner's jury investigating the tragic murder of 11-year old
Adjournment Debate
Christopher Stephenson reconvened and issued a statement at a press conference.
I think it is important to read the statement verbatim into the record of this House of Commons:
We spent four and one-half months listening to the testimony of approximately 90 witnesses before making our verdict and recommendations. We feel strongly that our 71 recommendations, if adopted, will preclude a tragedy of this nature from happening again.
Crucial and indispensable to these recommendations was the cross-examination of these witnesses by Mr. Tim Danson who represented Jim and Anna Stephenson. His consistent pursuit of the truth, from all witnesses, greatly benefited our decisions. Indeed, we cannot conceive of an inquest of this depth and nature proceeding without the perspective provided by Mr. Danson on behalf of the Stephensons who are the parents of Christopher, the victim.
The Solicitor General of Canada, the Honourable Doug Lewis, has publicly stated that Jim and Anna Stephenson did not need independent legal counsel and that had they come to him for legal advice he would have told the Stephensons this. Mr. Lewis also said that his decision to deny funding to the Stephensons was sensitive, sound and just. We disagree with both points. We think he is wrong. We therefore urge the minister to reconsider his position and we hope that he will consider our opinion in the positive and constructive way in which it has been given.
We therefore strongly recommend and urge the federal government and the provincial government to compensate Jim and Anna Stephenson for all legal costs incurred in this inquest, the results, if acted upon, will benefit all Canadian families.
We remind everyone that on June 17, 1988, Christopher Stephenson, age 11, went shopping with his mother at a local mall. They had every right in the world to be there. Joseph Fredericks who had spent 34 years in either mental or correctional institutions should not have been there. Mr. Danson made all this very clear to us.
The Solicitor General is obfuscating. The Solicitor General is stalling. He is talking about consulting with the bar association. He is talking about consulting with the Law Society of Upper Canada.
He does not need to consult because an independent jury of ordinary Canadians has already told him what to do. I quote the foreman:
We are the ones that were asked as citizens of this country to attend the inquest. I think we are probably the only ones who have the insight to recognize that the government should pick up the legal expenses for the Stephensons.
To suggest first of all that the taxpayer should not be paying the cost is a specious argument. All legal bills can be examined by the court to determine that they are fair and reasonable. To say that this will create a precedent is also nonsense. To make the payment and simply announce this is not a precedent ends it. There is precedent in legal history for this, and I cite it for the Canadian public now.

Adjournment Debate
Susan Nelles was paid an amount of money by the province of Ontario some time after her preliminary inquiry on a no-precedent basis. There is absolutely no reason why the Solicitor General cannot accept this recommendation by this jury.
The Toronto Sun said it best in an editorial:
Well, it is time to look after the interests of the victims. Federal
Solicitor General Doug Lewis and the provincial government can
start with the Stephensons.
I ask the Solicitor General to please pay the reasonable legal bill.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Solicitor General, like my hon. colleague, is sympathetic to the tragic loss experienced by the Stephensons and the efforts they have made to participate in the recent inquest in order to get the best possible results.
Consequently, on compassionate grounds, the government offered what it believed to be a reasonable settlement of their outstanding civil action against the Crown. That offer remains on the table.
With regard to the legal fees, the government has no idea what they amount to, because no final bill or account has been submitted by the family or their counsel. Let me be clear that the offer the government made to settle the law suit was not specifically to pay the legal fees, although the family would be free to use it for that purpose.
On the matter of the inquest itself, it should be noted that inquests are provincial mechanisms established at considerable cost, to protect the interests of citizens by ensuring that the causes of deaths are known and corrective action, where required, is recommended.
The federal government co-operated fully in this process, also at considerable expense. I believe my hon. colleague will understand that the offers, which are still on the table, should receive an answer at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, last week I had 11 constituents come into my riding office in Toronto. Seven out of those 11 constituents had lost their jobs. They were out of work. These were not habitual
receivers of unemployment insurance or welfare. Each of them in fact had worked all their adult life. All of them wanted to work.
The problem is that there is no work available for them. There is no work as an architect. There is no work as an optometrist's assistant. There is no work as a sales manager. There is no work in the hospitality industry. There is no work in computers. It goes on and on.
At the same time I walked out the front door of my office and looked across the street at the East York, North York O'Connor-Bermondsey industrial district. What did I see there? I saw the McBride Group plant for sale. I saw the CCL Industries plant for sale with a sign on the front "Job Search Assistance Committee-Action Centre". I saw the McLellan and Stewart plant for sale. I saw Halls Canada Paper closed. I saw Long Packaging closed and for sale. I saw Block Drug for sale or for lease. I saw Rockwell International for sale. The list goes on and on because one-third of all of the plants in that industrial area are closed.
This is the industrial heartland of Canada. These plants were used to generate wealth for Canada and used to generate federal tax dollars. What, if anything, is there that we can do? If there is something we can do where is the money going to come from?
It is interesting to note that about one-third of all of the green plan budget, which is about $1 billion, has not as yet been publicly committed. Rather than spending that money on more and more studies, why do we not use that money not only to clean up the environment but also to stimulate the economy and to create jobs at the same time?
This Friday metropolitan Toronto is holding an economic summit to try to find ways to get the economy going again. I am going to be there. Will the minister come and will he bring with him a handful of that green plan money?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the green plan makes an important contribution to both the environment and the economic future of this country by investing substantial resources in science, education, technology and other programs which will help us meet our environmental goals in ways that promote economic prosperity. There are many examples of how green plan funding will contribute to Canadian competitiveness.
February 16, 1993

For instance, in the forest sector the green plan commits the government to accelerate and intensify its efforts to develop and deploy environmentally sound solutions to the forest management for insects and disease. Reducing loss or damage will yield benefits to Canadians to enhance economic and recreational use of our forests.
The green plan also recognizes that private sector research and development of environmental technologies promises new investment opportunities and the creation of jobs in Canada's environmental industries.
The environmental technology industry is among the fastest growing sectors in the Canadian economy and it will play an increasing role in positioning Canada favourably in a highly competitive world market. That is why the green plan has initiated a program to accelerate the development and demonstration of commercially viable environmental technologies. That is also why additional green plan funds have been made available to assist Canadian firms in locating, assessing, transferring and promoting environmental technologies.
This government recognizes the important contribution of infrastructure projects to both job creation and to
Adjournment Debate
Canada's competitive position in the global economy. In its December economic statement, the government announced a strategic investment program which will encompass investments in all regions to strengthen our national transportation system and communications network.
Investments will include upgrade of federally owned highways, bridges, ports and airports, as well as development of a high-speed, high-capacity information network across the country.
Over the next five years these initiatives will result in investments in national infrastructure of more than $2 billion and are expected to generate 6,000 to 8,000 direct jobs each year.
